candidates.name: RAGFlow
candidates.what_it_is: Full RAG+agent platform. Template-based chunking, DeepDoc layout/OCR/table parsing, hybrid (full-text + vector) multi-recall with fused re-rank, traceable citations, chunk-visualisation UI. The 1.0 line (1.0.0-rc1 released 2026-09-29) is a rewrite to a Go-native service: DeepDoc runs inside the Go process via CGO + ONNX Runtime, on CPU only in open source. Default doc engine is Elasticsearch; Infinity (InfiniFlow's own C++ DB) is an alternative. Newer features: Knowledge Compilation (wiki/graph/tree/PageIndex artifacts), agentic multi-step retrieval, sitemap ingestion, incremental sync from data sources (e.g. BigQuery).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Closest full-stack analogue to our Rust service: parse -> chunk -> hybrid index -> cited retrieval, and it has just moved its core to a compiled language with native PDF/ONNX parsing, so its parsing/chunking templates and citation-position handling are worth reading. Its docs do NOT state a max document or chunk count, and do not document page/offset provenance in citations (WebFetch of the FAQ found none). A heavy stack (ES or Infinity + MySQL/Redis/MinIO); we would borrow ideas (layout-aware chunking templates, table handling), not adopt it.
candidates.scale_evidence: No documented corpus ceiling. Docs only give batch sizes (32 chunks per indexing batch), 1 GiB file-manager and 128 MiB dataset per-file upload limits, and a starting spec of 4 cores / 16 GB / 50 GB disk. Infinity vendor claim (unverified, vendor): 1 ms latency and 12K+ QPS full-text on 33M documents. No independent benchmark found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes. The 1.0 Go DeepDoc runs layout, OCR and table recognition on CPU (docs statement), but CPU parsing of 3-5M pages will be slow (unverified throughput).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Open-source 1.0 DeepDoc does not use GPU; GPU only for optional local embedding/LLM models.

candidates.name: LightRAG (HKUDS)
candidates.what_it_is: Dual-level (entity/relation graph + vector) retrieval. v1.5.x (latest release v1.5.7, 2026-09-02) added a pluggable parsing pipeline (MinerU, Docling, Native), four chunking strategies including a paragraph-semantic chunker that keeps headings, paragraphs and tables whole and can drop reference sections, multimodal (images/tables/formulas) processing, citation support (since 2025-03), incremental insert and selective delete using the LLM cache, and storage backends Postgres (recommended for production, serves all four stores), MongoDB, OpenSearch (added 2026-03), Neo4j, Milvus and others. REST API server + WebUI.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: It is the RAG engine inside our DeepTutor upstream (DeepTutor release notes mention native LightRAG role models and a published index that records what built it). The paragraph-semantic chunker and table/header-row-aware splitting are directly relevant to keeping equations and tables whole. Weakness for us: graph extraction needs one LLM call per chunk, which is prohibitive at 10-50M chunks on local hardware; the README itself says default in-memory stores are 'not for production'. Use as a reference for chunking and delete/rebuild semantics, not as the bulk index.
candidates.license: MIT per GitHub repo licence (note: the arXiv abstract page states CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0; repo LICENSE file should be checked before any reuse)
candidates.scale_evidence: No corpus size documented; README says 'supports large datasets' with Postgres and lists concurrency env vars for large-scale processing. Paper evaluated on small UltraDomain corpora (unverified sizes). EdgeQuake's own benchmark (n=200 medical questions, vendor-authored by a competitor) measured LightRAG at 1325 ms vs 5715 ms query latency.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Retrieval side yes; indexing is LLM-bound (entity extraction per chunk), a local LLM would be needed and is slow.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Local LLM entity extraction and embedding (the second GPU desktop); README recommends roughly 30B-class LLMs for good extraction.

candidates.name: RAG-Anything (HKUDS)
candidates.category: multimodal document RAG layer on LightRAG
candidates.what_it_is: Multimodal front-end for LightRAG: parses with MinerU, Docling or PaddleOCR, decomposes documents into text blocks, images, tables and equations (with LaTeX), runs dedicated processors per modality, builds a dual graph and does cross-modal hybrid retrieval. Paper 2510.12323 (2025-10-14).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Upstream of our DeepTutor fork. Its modality-specific handling of equations and tables, and equation-to-concept mapping, is the most relevant open design for maths/chemistry books. Same caveat: LLM/VLM calls per block make it impractical as the whole-corpus indexer; use selectively (e.g. for a curated subset of books).
candidates.scale_evidence: No scale claims in README; paper reports gains mainly on long multimodal documents (specific numbers not retrieved - unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Parsing with MinerU/Docling is possible on CPU but slow; VLM captioning of images/tables is not realistic on CPU at scale.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: MinerU/PaddleOCR layout+formula models (faster on GPU), VLM captioning, local LLM extraction.

candidates.name: PaperQA2 (Future-House/paper-qa)
candidates.what_it_is: Agentic RAG over local PDF/text repositories: parses and caches PDFs into a tantivy full-text index, embeddings in a NumPy vector DB by default, metadata-aware embeddings, LLM re-ranking and contextual summarisation (RCS) per chunk, iterative query refinement, in-text citations (e.g. Author2016 pages 1-2), metadata enrichment from Crossref / Semantic Scholar / Unpaywall, optional Docling readers and media-object support. CalVer releases since Dec 2025 (latest v2026.08.12).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Only mainstream framework here built around citation-with-page-range for science papers, and it uses tantivy (same as our Rust service). Its RCS re-rank/summarise step and citation format are a model for our conditional rerank and exact-quote citation checks. Index is file-based and incremental by diff (re-run skips unchanged papers) but not designed for 10K+ books: README advises API keys for metadata services at 100+ papers.
candidates.scale_evidence: No large-corpus figure documented; README guidance starts at 100+ papers. Paper (2409.13740, 2024-09-10) reports LitQA2 performance at or above expert level (vendor/author claim; LitQA2 is small, about tens of questions).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes for retrieval (tantivy + NumPy); LLM calls for RCS are the cost (would go to a local LLM).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Only optional local embedding models and the summarising LLM.

candidates.name: Onyx (formerly Danswer)
candidates.what_it_is: AI chat plus connector-driven enterprise search. Standard mode runs a vector+keyword index with background workers for connector sync, model inference servers for indexing/inference, Redis and MinIO. Migrating its document index from Vespa to OpenSearch (dual-indexing in v3, cloud fully on OpenSearch April 2026, Vespa deprecation planned v4). Permission-aware search is Enterprise-edition only.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Best public sizing guidance for a hybrid index at our size: docs give storage = source data x (1+replicas) x 1.45 and memory of about 1 GB per 1 GB of source docs at 50+ GB scale on OpenSearch. Useful as a cross-check of our memory/disk budget (tantivy on 100 GB free disk is tight for 50-250 GB of PDFs, since index size is driven by extracted text, not PDF bytes). Connector/permission model is enterprise-oriented and mostly not relevant.
candidates.license: MIT (Expat) except 'ee' directories under the Onyx Enterprise License; GitHub reports NOASSERTION
candidates.scale_evidence: Docs: recommended for under 5,000 users; sizing table by GB of indexed source data (vendor documentation, not a benchmark). No documented document-count ceiling.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Indexing servers can run embeddings on CPU; heavy stack (OpenSearch, Postgres, Redis, MinIO).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Optional: embedding and rerank inference servers.

candidates.name: CocoIndex
candidates.what_it_is: Declarative incremental data-transformation engine with a Rust core and Python API: functions are memoised by hash of input and code, so only the delta is recomputed when sources or code change; targets include Postgres/pgvector and other stores; parallel by default; includes text splitters and embedding ops.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Directly addresses our incremental-ingest requirement at larger scale: content-hash memoisation keyed on both input and pipeline code version (so a chunker change re-processes only affected files). Our BLAKE3 content-hash scheme is the same idea; CocoIndex shows how to track lineage/versioning of the transform as well. Worth reading for design, not for adoption (Python API, Postgres-centric).
candidates.scale_evidence: README claims 'any scale, parallel by default' (vendor claim, unverified); no corpus numbers found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes; orchestration only, cost is in the embed/parse functions you plug in.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Nothing itself; embedding/OCR functions you call.

candidates.name: Xberg (successor to Kreuzberg)
candidates.what_it_is: Rust-core document intelligence engine: 107 formats, PDFium-based PDF extraction, OCR backends (Tesseract, PaddleOCR, Candle, VLM), ML layout (PP-DocLayout-V3, RT-DETR) and table models (TATR, SLANet), Markdown/JSON/DocTags output, content-hash caching, parallel batch, local ONNX embeddings, sparse and late-interaction embeddings, cross-encoder reranking, REST/MCP/CLI, CPU by default.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Overlaps our PDFium extraction and lives in the same language, so it is a candidate crate or reference for the OCR fallback, table reconstruction and layout steps, and for bundling local ONNX embedding and rerank in the same binary. Not a RAG framework per se; listed because it is the strongest Rust entrant in the pipeline. Benchmarks are on the vendor's site (xberg.io/benchmarks, not reviewed, unverified). Young v1 rebrand of Kreuzberg.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim 'fastest, most precise' with no independent benchmark reviewed; no corpus size documented.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes, CPU by default, no GPU required (vendor statement).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Optional: faster OCR/layout via ONNX/CUDA; VLM OCR backend.

candidates.name: PageIndex (VectifyAI)
candidates.what_it_is: Builds a hierarchical table-of-contents tree per document and has an LLM reason over the tree to pick sections (with page numbers), instead of chunk embeddings. Local mode benchmark in README: indexing about 13 s to 4.5 min for 9 to 1,098 page PDFs (vendor numbers) and 62 lookup questions over 34 PDFs (1,945 pages). The 'File System' layer for millions of documents is Enterprise/Cloud only, not open source. RAGFlow and DeepTutor (v1.5.2) have both adopted PageIndex-style retrieval.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Books have real chapter/section structure and our chunks already carry heading paths, so a tree-navigation retrieval mode is a cheap add-on for guided reading and for whole-chapter proofs/derivations, with page-accurate provenance. LLM-per-query and per-document indexing cost makes it unsuitable as the primary index at 10M+ chunks; use as a second-stage over BM25-selected books.
candidates.license: MIT (OSS); File System layer is proprietary
candidates.scale_evidence: OSS README benchmarks only up to 1,098-page documents; millions-of-documents claim is for the closed File System product and its launch post provides no benchmark numbers.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes (LLM API or local LLM calls; no local models required).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Local LLM if not using an API (the second desktop).

candidates.name: Microsoft GraphRAG
candidates.what_it_is: LLM extracts entities, relationships and claims, runs community detection and generates multi-level community summaries; search modes Global, Local, DRIFT and basic; output as Parquet tables plus a vector store. v3.2.0 released 2026-09-24. README now explicitly describes it as a research project and 'not an officially supported Microsoft offering', and warns that indexing is expensive.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Global sensemaking queries (e.g. 'themes across these 200 organic chemistry texts') are not what our tutor needs most; indexing cost (LLM calls for every chunk plus community summaries) is prohibitive at 10-50M chunks. Not recommended beyond reading the incremental/community-summary ideas.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper (arXiv 2404.16130, 2024-04-24, v2 2025-02-19) evaluated on corpora in the 1 million token range; no larger documented scale (paper abstract page).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Pipeline runs on CPU but is LLM-call bound.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Local LLM for extraction and summarisation; embeddings.

candidates.name: LlamaIndex
candidates.what_it_is: Data framework with 300+ integration packages (LLMs, embeddings, vector stores), node parsers, ingestion pipelines with caching and doc-hash dedupe, retrievers, query engines. The company has pivoted to LlamaParse (hosted agentic OCR, 130+ formats); README now says 'the document processing platform for AI' and describes the OSS framework as playing a supporting role.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Reference vocabulary and abstractions (node relationships, hierarchical/auto-merging retrieval, fusion retriever) we can reimplement in Rust; DeepTutor already uses it for ingestion. The best parser (LlamaParse) is cloud-only, which our no-cloud rule excludes.
candidates.scale_evidence: No corpus-size claim in README; scale depends entirely on the chosen vector store.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Nothing inherent; local embedding and rerank models if used.

candidates.name: Haystack (deepset)
candidates.what_it_is: Explicit Pipeline graph of components (retrievers, rankers, converters, splitters, evaluators) with sync/async execution, branches and loops; document stores for Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Qdrant, Weaviate, pgvector and others via integrations; Hayhooks serves pipelines as REST/MCP; managed Enterprise platform offered.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Clean component boundaries (converter -> splitter -> embedder -> writer; BM25 + embedding retrievers -> joiner (RRF) -> ranker) that match what we already built; good as a checklist and for its built-in evaluators. Nothing here beats our Rust index at our scale.
candidates.scale_evidence: No documented corpus ceiling in README; scale delegated to the document store.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: Kotaemon (Cinnamon)
candidates.what_it_is: Gradio app with hybrid (full-text + vector) retriever and re-ranking by default, in-browser PDF viewer with highlighted citations and relevance scores, multi-user, optional GraphRAG/NanoGraphRAG/LightRAG indexing. Latest release v0.12.0 (2026-05-31); last commit 2026-05-30.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Its PDF-viewer citation highlighting is the closest UI reference for exact page/offset citations. Slowing maintenance (last commit about four months ago) and Gradio/Python make it a UI reference only.
candidates.scale_evidence: None documented; aimed at small personal/team document sets.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes (can run local GGUF models via llama-cpp).

candidates.name: txtai
candidates.what_it_is: Embeddings database combining sparse and dense vector indexes, graph networks and a relational store (SQLite/DuckDB-style SQL over vectors), plus RAG, agents and workflows. Low footprint, runs locally.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: A compact single-process reference for hybrid sparse+dense index with SQL filtering and graph; author publishes a 'running txtai at scale' article (not reviewed). Not sized for tens of millions of chunks without sharding (unverified).
candidates.scale_evidence: No corpus size in README; links a Medium article on running at scale (not reviewed, unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: R2R (SciPhi)
candidates.what_it_is: Postgres-backed retrieval system with hybrid search, knowledge graphs, RAG with citations, Deep Research agent, REST API.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Appears stalled: last commit 2025-11-07 and latest release v3.6.5 on 2025-06-06, versus near-daily commits for peers. Not worth adopting; historically useful only as an example of Postgres full-text + pgvector hybrid in one DB.
candidates.scale_evidence: None documented.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: Morphik Core
candidates.what_it_is: Multimodal retrieval using ColPali-style visual document embeddings, metadata extraction with bounding boxes, integrations (Google, Slack, Confluence); hosted service with free tier.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: ColPali-style page-image retrieval is a possible later approach for scanned pages and diagrams once the GPU desktop exists. Licence is Business Source License 1.1 (production use free only under US$2,000/month of attributable revenue), so a licence flag for anything but personal use.
candidates.scale_evidence: None documented; vendor marketing only.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Poor: visual embeddings are GPU-oriented.

candidates.name: Khoj
candidates.what_it_is: Self-hostable assistant over personal documents and the web with agents, automations and deep research.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Personal-scale semantic search over notes; AGPL-3.0 and last commit 2026-08-02 (two months ago). Not relevant to a 10K-book library; licence flag.
candidates.scale_evidence: None documented.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes for small corpora.

candidates.name: Dify
candidates.category: LLM app platform with knowledge bases
candidates.what_it_is: Workflow/agent builder with knowledge-base ingestion and many vector-DB back ends; most-starred project in this landscape.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Adoption signal only. Licence is a modified Apache 2.0 that forbids running a multi-tenant service and removing logo/copyright without written permission. Knowledge-base internals are generic chunk+embed; not a citation-precise library engine.
candidates.license: Modified Apache-2.0 with multi-tenant and logo restrictions (flag)
candidates.scale_evidence: None documented for KB size.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: FastGPT
candidates.what_it_is: Chinese-origin knowledge-base QA platform: TXT/MD/HTML/PDF/Docx/PPTX/CSV/XLSX loaders, chunk editing, hybrid retrieval, visual flow orchestration.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Strong Chinese-language tuning may be useful as a Mandarin reference; same modified-Apache restrictions as Dify (no multi-tenant SaaS, keep logo).
candidates.scale_evidence: None documented in README.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: QAnything (NetEase Youdao)
candidates.what_it_is: Pure-CPU-capable local KB QA with independent replaceable components (PDF parse, OCR, embed, rerank) and two-stage retrieval (vector recall then rerank); claims no limit on uploaded files and that retrieval quality improves with more data.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Design precedent for two-stage retrieve-then-rerank on CPU and Chinese/English cross-lingual QA (their BCEmbedding/reranker models). AGPL-3.0 is a licence flag; the scale claim is marketing (vendor, unverified).
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim 'massive data, no limit on number of files' (unverified, no numbers).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes, defaults to pure CPU (vendor claim).

candidates.name: EdgeQuake
candidates.what_it_is: 11-crate Rust workspace (axum API) implementing the LightRAG algorithm over PostgreSQL 16-18 with pgvector and Apache AGE, pdfium-based text extraction plus an optional vision PDF mode, durable Postgres-backed ingestion queue, auth, audit, OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/Mistral/Ollama providers. v0.28.5.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: The only sizeable Rust RAG server of this shape (axum + pdfium) and therefore the nearest existing code to our stack. Its own benchmark (n=200, medical) shows a statistical tie with LightRAG on accuracy (0.792 vs 0.786) but 4.3x slower queries (5715 ms vs 1325 ms), so the Rust rewrite did not win on latency. Single-maintainer project with 2.1K stars; read for PDF page-as-unit conversion and Postgres task-queue patterns only.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor benchmark only (n=200 questions); no corpus-size claim.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes apart from the LLM extraction calls.

candidates.name: LEANN
candidates.what_it_is: Graph-based vector index that recomputes embeddings on the fly rather than storing them (HNSW or DiskANN backends); README cites 60M Wikipedia chunks in 6 GB versus 201 GB for a conventional index (vendor claim). Semantic-only: no BM25/hybrid; recompute needs a GPU for reasonable latency.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Directly relevant to the 100 GB free-disk limit once dense vectors are added (10-50M chunks x 768-1024 dims is tens to hundreds of GB). The catch is that query-time recompute needs the embedding GPU, which we do not have yet. Watch; evaluate after the second desktop exists.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor/paper claim: 60M chunks in 6 GB (Wikipedia). Paper arXiv 2506.08276 (v1 2025-06-09, v2 2025-11-25) reports up to 50x storage reduction (authors). README says MLSys 2026 best paper (vendor statement, unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Searching is possible on CPU but slow because embeddings are recomputed (README says GPU recommended).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: On-the-fly embedding recompute at query time.

candidates.name: Infinity (InfiniFlow)
candidates.category: AI-native hybrid search database (RAGFlow's alternative doc engine)
candidates.what_it_is: C++ database with dense, sparse, tensor (multi-vector) and full-text search in one engine.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Vendor claims 1 ms latency and 12K+ QPS on full-text search over 33M documents and 0.1 ms / 15K+ QPS on million-scale dense search (unverified, vendor). Gives a reference point for the FTS-at-tens-of-millions target and shows BM25 at 33M documents is an accepted scale for purpose-built engines; our tantivy index should reach that scale too (tantivy is a mature Rust Lucene-class engine, not reviewed here).
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim: 33M documents full-text (unverified; benchmark report not reviewed).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: AnythingLLM
candidates.what_it_is: Workspace-based document chat app with bundled vector DB (LanceDB default) and many providers; MIT, very active (last push 2026-09-30).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Adoption signal and a local-first UX reference; not designed for 10K+ book corpora or page-accurate citations.
candidates.scale_evidence: None documented.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: Zleap SAG
candidates.what_it_is: Knowledge base application built on the SAG architecture: event-entity indexing with query-time dynamic hyperedges using SQL joins on shared entities, source tracing, cited answers, API/MCP. Paper arXiv 2606.15971 (2026-06-14, rev 2026-08-25) reports 80.36% Recall@5 on MuSiQue, 11.52 points above the strongest baseline (authors' claim).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: New (about 2.5K stars) and claims SOTA on multi-hop QA using a relational store instead of a graph DB, which is cheap to run, but it needs LLM event/entity extraction for every document and its benchmarks are the small multi-hop QA sets, not book-scale. Watch only.
candidates.scale_evidence: Only HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue (small sets); no large-corpus claim.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Retrieval yes; extraction is LLM-bound.

candidates.name: PipesHub
candidates.what_it_is: Apache-2.0 platform with 50+ connectors (real-time and scheduled indexing), permission-aware search, cited answers with page-level provenance claims, MCP and SDKs.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Connector-centric and enterprise-oriented; little for a static book library. Noted as a newer entrant with strong adoption growth signals (about 3.8K stars).
candidates.scale_evidence: None documented.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes (unverified).

papers.title: LightRAG: Simple and Fast Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.key_result: Dual-level graph+vector retrieval with an incremental update algorithm; reports better retrieval accuracy and response time than baselines such as GraphRAG (specific figures not retrieved; unverified). EMNLP 2025 per repo.

papers.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
papers.key_result: Substantial gains over conventional RAG in comprehensiveness and diversity of answers on global sensemaking questions; evaluated on datasets in the 1 million token range.

papers.title: Language agents achieve superhuman synthesis of scientific knowledge (PaperQA2)
papers.key_result: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on literature tasks; introduces LitQA2; Wikipedia-style summaries judged more accurate than human-written Wikipedia articles; about 2.34 contradictions found per biology paper with 70% expert-validated (authors' claims).

papers.title: RAG-Anything: All-in-One RAG Framework
papers.key_result: Dual-graph construction and cross-modal hybrid retrieval over text, images, tables and equations; reports substantial gains on multimodal benchmarks, especially long documents (numbers not retrieved; unverified).

papers.title: LEANN: A Low-Storage Vector Index
papers.key_result: Up to 50x storage reduction (index about 5% of raw data) at comparable latency and accuracy by recomputing embeddings on the fly; README example 60M Wikipedia chunks in 6 GB vs 201 GB.

papers.title: SAG: SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation with Query-Time Dynamic Hyperedges
papers.key_result: 80.36% Recall@5 on MuSiQue, 11.52 points above the strongest baseline; gains on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA (authors' claim; small multi-hop benchmarks).

findings: No open RAG framework reviewed documents a corpus near our 10-50M chunk target. Stated limits are small: GraphRAG paper about 1M tokens; PaperQA2 guidance starts at 100+ papers; RAGFlow, LightRAG, Haystack, LlamaIndex, Khoj, Dify, FastGPT, Kotaemon and R2R give no corpus ceiling; QAnything claims 'no limit' without numbers (vendor). Scale is delegated to the index store (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Infinity, Postgres, Milvus), so our own tantivy-based service is on the same footing as these frameworks for scale, and ahead of them for CPU-only BM25 over large local PDF sets.

The only hard sizing data found: Onyx docs give storage = source data x (1+replicas) x 1.45 and about 1 GB RAM per GB of source docs at 50+ GB on OpenSearch (vendor docs). Infinity claims 1 ms / 12K+ QPS full-text on 33M documents (vendor, unverified). Use both only as cross-checks; neither is an independent benchmark.

Graph-RAG family (GraphRAG, LightRAG, RAG-Anything, EdgeQuake, SAG, nano-graphrag) needs an LLM call per chunk or more at index time. At 10-50M chunks this is infeasible locally without the planned GPU machine, and the benefit targets multi-hop and global questions rather than exact-citation lookup. Microsoft itself now labels GraphRAG a research demo, not a supported product. Recommendation: keep BM25 + optional vectors as the base, and reserve graph/tree methods for small curated subsets.

Trend in the landscape: RAGFlow moved to a Go-native core with in-process ONNX/CGO parsing (1.0.0-rc1, 2026-09-29); LlamaIndex pivoted its company to hosted LlamaParse; Onyx is replacing Vespa with OpenSearch; LightRAG added a paragraph-semantic chunker that keeps tables and headings whole plus pluggable parsers (MinerU, Docling). Several projects (RAGFlow, DeepTutor, PageIndex) are converging on vectorless tree/PageIndex-style retrieval using document structure, which fits books with heading paths and page ranges that we already store.

Rust is where the incremental/ingest and extraction building blocks are appearing: CocoIndex (Rust core, memoised incremental engine, 11.6K stars), Xberg/Kreuzberg (Rust extraction engine with PDFium, ONNX layout/table models, local embeddings and rerank, MIT, 9.4K stars), plus fastembed-rs (1.0K stars) and pdf_oxide (1.1K stars) seen in a GitHub search (not reviewed in depth). Chunkr (Rust, 4.2K stars) is AGPL-3.0 and should be avoided for reuse.

Licence flags: Khoj and QAnything are AGPL-3.0; Chunkr is AGPL-3.0; Morphik is Business Source License 1.1; Dify and FastGPT are modified Apache with multi-tenant and logo restrictions; Onyx is MIT except the 'ee' directories; MinerU is Apache-2.0 plus additional terms (separate licence above 100M MAU or US$20M monthly revenue; online-service attribution); Open WebUI and MinerU report NOASSERTION on GitHub (custom licence). LightRAG's repo is MIT per GitHub but its arXiv abstract page says CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0, so check the LICENSE file in the clone before copying code.

Star snapshot on 2026-09-30 (GitHub API): Dify 157.6K, RAGFlow 91.6K, AnythingLLM 66.6K, LlamaIndex 52.4K, DeepTutor 40.6K, LightRAG 39.9K, PageIndex 38.1K, Khoj 37.5K, GraphRAG 36.2K, Onyx 32.3K, FastGPT 29.8K, Haystack 26.6K, Kotaemon 25.8K, RAG-Anything 23.5K, QAnything 14.2K, txtai 13.0K, LEANN 13.0K, PaperQA2 9.3K, R2R 8.0K. Growth rate over time could not be measured (no star history retrieved); the fast-rising names visible by recency and star count are PageIndex, LEANN, RAG-Anything, CocoIndex, Xberg and SAG.

Stale or slowing: R2R (last commit 2025-11-07, last release 2025-06-06), Kotaemon (last commit 2026-05-30), Khoj (2026-08-02), Weaviate Verba (archived), nano-graphrag (2026-01-27), MiniRAG (2025-10-16). Do not build on these.

Citation provenance gap: among the frameworks reviewed, only PaperQA2 (pages per context, e.g. 'pages 1-2'), Kotaemon (PDF viewer highlights) and LightRAG (citation feature since 2025-03) document citations that point back into the source. None documents exact-quote verification or byte/character offset provenance, which our service already does with heading paths, page ranges and exact-quote checks. Equations and tables are handled by parser choice (MinerU, Docling, DeepDoc, Xberg), not by the framework.

Top 8 to clone in depth (worth_cloning true): RAGFlow (Go-native parsing/chunking templates), LightRAG (paragraph-semantic chunker, delete/rebuild), RAG-Anything (equation/table handling), PaperQA2 (tantivy + cited contexts + RCS), Onyx (hybrid index sizing, OpenSearch move), CocoIndex (incremental memoised ingest), Xberg (Rust extraction/layout/OCR chain), and, if only 8 are wanted, treat PageIndex as the first next pick.

No repository was cloned, installed or modified."

candidates.name: NextPlaid / ColGREP (lightonai)
candidates.what_it_is: Rust multi-vector (ColBERT MaxSim) search engine with memory-mapped indexes, 2-bit/4-bit product quantisation, incremental add/delete, SQLite metadata filtering, and built-in ONNX Runtime encoding. ColGREP is a code-search CLI on top. Release 1.7.0.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Only actively maintained Rust late-interaction engine found. It can rerank BM25 top-k or index a curated subset (math/chemistry notes). The Rust stack matches our service. Whole-corpus indexing is probably too large for 100 GB disk (see findings).
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor README only: BEIR with GTE-ModernColBERT-v1, CPU about 17 QPS with P95 about 250 ms; GPU about 21 QPS; indexing 105.5 docs/s on H100. BEIR corpora are small, so there is no 10M+ chunk evidence (unverified at our scale).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes for search (README claims CPU-optimised). Query encoding with a 150M ColBERT is feasible via ONNX; bulk document encoding of millions of chunks on CPU is slow.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Bulk document encoding (indexing) at scale; optional CUDA in the library.

candidates.name: BGE-Reasoner / ReasonEmbed / Retro-star (VectorSpaceLab agentic-search)
candidates.what_it_is: Open end-to-end BRIGHT pipeline: Qwen2.5-7B query rewriter (5 rewrites), BGE-Reasoner-Embed (Qwen3-4B/8B, RI-InfoNCE loss, 37-38 nDCG@10 on original queries), BM25 over 2000 candidates, score-sum across rewrites, 0.75/0.25 min-max fusion of dense and BM25, and 8B/14B/32B reasoning rerankers. BRIGHT 46.4 (Oct 2025). Training data and search results released.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Best fully reproducible recipe for reasoning-heavy math/science queries. The portable parts on CPU are the BM25 side, multi-rewrite score summing, and convex fusion. The embedder and reranker need GPU. The data and recipes suit the future GPU desktop.
candidates.license: MIT (repo). Model licences: BAAI embed Apache-2.0 on HF; other checkpoints not checked.
candidates.scale_evidence: BRIGHT (1,384 queries, 12 sub-corpora, small) self-reported and released with search results. No library-scale evidence.
candidates.cpu_feasible: BM25 part yes. Rewriter 7B on CPU is slow but usable for query-time only (seconds to tens of seconds, unverified). Embedder and reranker 8B+ are impractical on CPU.

candidates.name: BrowseComp-Plus
candidates.what_it_is: Fixed ~100K human-verified-document corpus with BrowseComp queries; separates retriever and LLM-agent effects; retrieval-only and agent tracks; prebuilt BM25 and Qwen3-Embedding indexes; reports nDCG@10, Recall@5/100/1000 and citation accuracy.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Template for our held-out audit sets: fixed corpus, evidence vs gold documents, retrieval-only and end-to-end tracks, citation accuracy scored separately. The reference for testing multi-hop agentic search over our library.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper (arXiv 2508.06600, Aug 2025): GPT-5 with BM25 55.9%, with Qwen3-Embedding-8B 70.1%; Search-R1 with BM25 3.86%. Independent academic benchmark.
candidates.cpu_feasible: BM25 track yes. Agent track needs LLM API or local LLM.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Qwen3-Embedding-8B index and local LLM agents.

candidates.name: FlagEmbedding (BGE-M3, bge-reranker-v2-m3, BGE-Reasoner base)
candidates.what_it_is: BAAI toolkit. BGE-M3 (MIT) gives dense, learned-sparse and ColBERT multi-vector output from one 568M model, 100+ languages, 8192-token input. Includes bge-reranker-v2-m3 (Apache-2.0), fine-tuning code, and MIRACL/MKQA/MLDR evaluation.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Most licence-clean single model covering Japanese, Chinese, Spanish, French and German with a sparse head that can feed a Rust inverted index (seismic or tantivy) and a multi-vector head for rerank. Good default for the multilingual dense and sparse lane once a GPU desktop exists.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper arXiv 2402.03216 (v. Dec 2025) claims SOTA on MIRACL, MKQA, MLDR (vendor numbers, not re-verified here). bge-m3 HF downloads about 35.7M, widely adopted.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Embedding 568M on CPU is roughly tens of chunks per second (unverified); fine for queries and small batches, too slow for 10-50M chunks.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Bulk encoding of millions of chunks, reranker throughput.

candidates.name: Seismic (TusKANNy)
candidates.what_it_is: Rust inverted index with block summary vectors for approximate retrieval over learned sparse vectors (SPLADE, BGE-M3 sparse and similar).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: If we adopt learned sparse vectors, this is the Rust index built for them, which tantivy does not do efficiently. It could sit beside tantivy BM25 and give expansion-style matching without dense-vector storage cost.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper arXiv 2404.18812 (Apr 2024): sub-millisecond per-query latency on MS MARCO (8.8M passages), 1-2 orders of magnitude faster than other inverted-index solutions, beats BigANN 2023 sparse track winners. Authors' own benchmark.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes; index and query are CPU-native. Producing the sparse vectors (SPLADE/BGE-M3 encoder) is the expensive step.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Only the encoder producing sparse vectors for documents.

candidates.name: PyLate (lightonai) with GTE-ModernColBERT and Reason-ModernColBERT
candidates.what_it_is: Sentence-Transformers-based ColBERT training and retrieval library (arXiv 2508.03555). Models: GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 (149M, Apache-2.0, BEIR 54.67), ColBERT-Zero (about 100M, Apache-2.0, BEIR 55.43 nDCG@10 under 150M params), Reason-ModernColBERT (150M, CC-BY-NC-4.0, BRIGHT mean 22.62 with 100K training samples).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: The best route to a small (about 150M) CPU-tolerant late-interaction reranker or retriever; a small late-interaction model beat 7B dense models on BRIGHT in the model card's own comparison (vendor claim). Note that Reason-ModernColBERT is non-commercial.
candidates.license: MIT (library); models vary (Apache-2.0 for GTE-ModernColBERT and ColBERT-Zero; CC-BY-NC-4.0 for Reason-ModernColBERT)
candidates.scale_evidence: Model-card numbers only (vendor). No 10M+ scale evidence.
candidates.cpu_feasible: 150M models run on CPU at query time; bulk encoding slow.

candidates.name: PaperQA2 (Future-House/paper-qa)
candidates.what_it_is: Agentic RAG over PDFs: LLM-driven query rewrite, retrieval, per-chunk re-ranking and contextual summarisation, citation traversal, and cited answers. Introduced the LitQA2 benchmark.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Closest open design to our tutor: citation-grounded answers with page-level provenance and an answer-only-from-evidence discipline. It is a source of ideas for our rerank, contextual summary and citation-check steps. Not designed for millions of documents.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper arXiv 2409.13740 (Sep 2024): PaperQA2 matches or beats experts on three literature tasks; about 70% of found contradictions validated (authors' own evaluation, independent replication not checked).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Retrieval side yes; quality depends on an LLM (local or API).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Nothing required; local LLM would need it.

candidates.name: BRIGHT benchmark harness (xlang-ai/BRIGHT)
candidates.what_it_is: 1,384 reasoning-intensive queries over 12 sub-corpora (StackExchange, coding, theorem-based math); data CC-BY-4.0; leaderboard at brightbenchmark.github.io. Paper: best MTEB model 59.0 on MTEB drops to 18.3 nDCG@10 on BRIGHT; explicit reasoning queries add up to 12.2 points.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Fast, small, CPU-runnable BM25 test for math/science reasoning queries, including rewrite-versus-original comparisons; use it for our eval with a held-out split alongside our own audit set.
candidates.scale_evidence: Independent academic benchmark; small corpora, so it says nothing about 10M+ chunk scale.
candidates.cpu_feasible: BM25 track yes.

candidates.name: Qwen3-Embedding / Qwen3-Reranker
candidates.what_it_is: 0.6B, 4B and 8B embedders and rerankers, Apache-2.0, 100+ languages, 32k context, MRL dimensions 32-4096, instruction-aware. 8B embedder MTEB multilingual 70.58 (June 2025, vendor claim), MTEB English v2 75.22, C-MTEB 73.84. Qwen3-Reranker-8B: MMTEB-R 72.94, CMTEB-R 77.45, MLDR 70.19.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Permissive, multilingual, strong default. 0.6B embedder (9.7M HF downloads) is the practical size for CPU query encoding and a modest GPU box. MRL lets us store 256-512-d vectors to cut disk. Used as the dense baseline in BrowseComp-Plus.
candidates.license: Apache-2.0 (HF model cards); GitHub repo shows no licence file
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor MTEB numbers. Independent adoption: BrowseComp-Plus uses the 8B embedder as its dense baseline.
candidates.cpu_feasible: 0.6B: query encoding yes. Bulk encoding of tens of millions of chunks no (unverified throughput).

candidates.name: microsoft/harrier-oss-v1 family
candidates.what_it_is: Microsoft embedding family (270M, 0.6B, 27B), MIT licence, 32k context, about 40 languages including Japanese, Chinese, Spanish, French, German. MTEB v2 multilingual 69.0 for 0.6B and 74.3 for 27B (model-card claim, not independently verified).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: MIT-licensed and small; 0.6B at 69.0 nearly matches Qwen3-Embedding-8B's 70.58. A strong candidate to benchmark against Qwen3-0.6B on our own multilingual set.
candidates.scale_evidence: Model card only (vendor).
candidates.cpu_feasible: 270M and 0.6B feasible for queries.

candidates.name: IBM granite-embedding-311m-multilingual-r2
candidates.what_it_is: 311M encoder, Apache-2.0, 32k context, 52 enhanced languages, multilingual MTEB Retrieval 65.2 (vendor claim); a 97M sibling exists.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Small, clean-licence, long-context multilingual option for a CPU-friendly first dense lane.
candidates.scale_evidence: Model card only (vendor).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes for 97M/311M at modest throughput (unverified).

candidates.name: INF-X-Retriever (infly)
candidates.what_it_is: Query Aligner (Qwen2.5-7B, RL-tuned intent extraction) plus inf-retriever-v1-pro (7B), no reranker, no HyDE. BRIGHT 63.4 (Dec 20, 2025); both models Apache-2.0 on HF.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Shows a no-reranker single-stage route to strong BRIGHT scores; repo has no licence file though HF models say Apache-2.0. Useful as a reference for RL-trained query rewriting.
candidates.license: none on repo; Apache-2.0 on HF model cards
candidates.scale_evidence: Self-reported leaderboard entry; not independently reproduced here.
candidates.cpu_feasible: No for 7B retriever at scale; the aligner could run per query on CPU slowly.

candidates.name: Mira-Reasoning-Retrieval (Forward AI Labs: MQR-A1 + MRE-T1)
candidates.what_it_is: GRPO-trained query rewriter (MQR-A1) plus dense retriever (MRE-T1); listed first on BRIGHT at 66.9 (short-document track), 56.0 long (Apr 22, 2026). Weights on HF under Apache-2.0 tag; no code link found; model sizes not stated.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Current BRIGHT leader, but very new, with almost no downloads (0 and 0 on HF) and no code. Treat as unverified; shows that RL-trained rewriting plus a dense retriever is the dominant 2026 pattern.
candidates.scale_evidence: Leaderboard self-report only (unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Unknown.

candidates.name: ReasonIR (facebookresearch)
candidates.what_it_is: ReasonIR-8B bi-encoder trained on synthetic reasoning queries with hard negatives. BRIGHT 29.9 nDCG@10 (36.9 with reranker); RAG gains of 6.4% MMLU and 22.6% GPQA. Paper arXiv 2504.20595 (Apr 2025).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Landmark synthetic-data recipe, now surpassed. Non-commercial (CC-BY-NC-4.0 model, FAIR NC repo) and the repo is reported archived, so use only as reading.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper numbers (authors).
candidates.cpu_feasible: No (8B).

candidates.name: Rank1 (orionw/rank1) and rank1-7b
candidates.what_it_is: Pointwise reranker distilled from 600K R1 reasoning traces on MS MARCO; models 0.5B to 7B (rank1-7b MIT); quantised versions keep accuracy. CoLM 2025 (arXiv 2502.18418).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Explainable reranker that also yields a reasoning trace for tutor use; smaller variants are plausible as a conditional reranker on CPU for the top-20, slowly (unverified). Test-time compute makes latency high.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper results on BRIGHT and instruction-following sets (authors); small scale.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Small models maybe, slow (long generated reasoning per document).

candidates.name: ReasonRank (8421BCD)
candidates.what_it_is: Listwise reasoning reranker trained by R1-synthesised labels plus RL with a multi-view ranking reward; BRIGHT 40.8 on the leaderboard (Aug 2025); ACL 2026 (arXiv 2508.07050).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Listwise reranking cuts latency versus pointwise reasoning rerankers; fits a conditional top-20 rerank. Needs GPU for 7B/32B.
candidates.scale_evidence: BRIGHT leaderboard self-report.
candidates.cpu_feasible: No for 7B+.

candidates.name: ielab/llm-rankers (Rank-R1, setwise/pairwise/listwise)
candidates.what_it_is: Reference implementations of pointwise, pairwise, setwise and Rank-R1 (RL-trained reasoning setwise reranker; arXiv 2503.06034, Mar 2025).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Setwise prompting reduces LLM calls; Rank-R1 reaches SFT-level in-domain quality with 18% of the data and does better out of domain with 14B models (authors).
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper on TREC DL and BRIGHT (authors).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Small LLMs only, slow.

candidates.name: Search-R1 (PeterGriffinJin)
candidates.what_it_is: RL (PPO/GRPO) framework training LLMs to issue multi-turn search queries with retrieved-token masking; +41% (Qwen2.5-7B) and +20% (3B) over RAG baselines on 7 QA sets (arXiv 2503.09516, Mar 2025). Supports BM25 and dense retrievers.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Reference design for the search-tool loop. However BrowseComp-Plus reports Search-R1 with BM25 at only 3.86% while GPT-5 reaches 55.9%, so small RL agents are far behind frontier models on hard multi-hop tasks.
candidates.scale_evidence: Academic benchmarks (Wikipedia-scale QA corpora) plus BrowseComp-Plus independent result.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Training no; inference of 3B-7B agent slow on CPU.

candidates.name: ReSearch / R1-Searcher / DeepResearcher / ASearcher / WebThinker / Tongyi DeepResearch
candidates.what_it_is: Successor agents. Agent-RL/ReSearch (1441 stars, MIT, NeurIPS 2025), RUCAIBox/R1-Searcher (727, MIT), GAIR-NLP/DeepResearcher (801, Apache-2.0, trains on the live web; +28.9 points over prompting), inclusionAI/ASearcher (613, no licence shown; 100+ tool calls, xBench 51.1, GAIA 58.7), RUC-NLPIR/WebThinker (1471, MIT), Alibaba-NLP/DeepResearch (20003, Apache-2.0, last push 2026-02-27).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: These mostly target the open web rather than a fixed local library and need GPU training. Useful ideas: multi-turn query reformulation, long tool-call horizons. Not recommended to adopt; a prompted loop over our own search tool is cheaper.
candidates.scale_evidence: Academic benchmarks (GAIA, xBench, QA sets), authors' own.
candidates.cpu_feasible: No for training; inference needs a local LLM.

candidates.name: jina-ai/late-chunking
candidates.what_it_is: Late chunking: embed the whole document with a long-context model, then pool token vectors per chunk (arXiv 2409.04701, revised July 2025). No training needed.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Cheaper than LLM contextualisation but needs a long-context embedder run over full documents; a comparison study (arXiv 2504.19754) found contextual retrieval better at keeping semantic coherence and late chunking cheaper but less complete.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper and small benchmarks; no library-scale evidence.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Only with small long-context models; full-document passes are costly.

candidates.name: Anthropic contextual retrieval (claude-cookbooks)
candidates.what_it_is: Prepend an LLM-written 50-100 token situating context to each chunk before embedding and BM25 (Sep 19, 2024). Failed retrievals fall 35% (embeddings), 49% (plus BM25), 67% (plus reranking); cost $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Directly applicable to BM25 fields. Vendor numbers, on their own datasets, with 800-token chunks. At 10-50M chunks a per-chunk LLM pass is not feasible on CPU, so restrict it to high-value sources or use cheaper context (title, heading path, section summary) which we already partly have.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim only, not independently reproduced.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Technique itself needs an LLM per chunk; local small LLM on CPU too slow at scale.

candidates.name: lindera-tantivy and tantivy-jieba
candidates.what_it_is: Japanese (Lindera, 678 stars, MIT, active 2026-09-30) and Chinese (jiegec/tantivy-jieba, 68 stars, MIT) tokenizers for tantivy; lindera-tantivy 70 stars, pushed 2026-08-07.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Without a CJK tokenizer, BM25 on Japanese and Mandarin is poor; these are drop-in Rust options. Quality on retrieval benchmarks not measured by me (unverified).
candidates.scale_evidence: None found for retrieval quality.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: License traps: SPLADE-v3, jina models, Reason-ModernColBERT, EmbeddingGemma, Nemotron embed, LFM ColBERT
candidates.what_it_is: naver/splade-v3 is CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 (repo naver/splade 1015 stars, last push 2024-05-03, NOASSERTION); jina-colbert-v2 and jina-reranker-v3 are CC-BY-NC-4.0; jina-embeddings-v5-omni-small CC-BY-NC-4.0; ReasonIR-8B CC-BY-NC-4.0; Reason-ModernColBERT CC-BY-NC-4.0; embeddinggemma-300m uses the Gemma licence; llama-embed-nemotron-8b is 'other'; LFM2.5-ColBERT is the LFM Open License v1.0.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: SPLADE-v3 is the usual learned-sparse baseline but non-commercial; BGE-M3 sparse (MIT) is the clean alternative. Personal use may be acceptable to the owner, but rights flags matter if the library is ever shared.
candidates.scale_evidence: SPLADE-v3 report (arXiv 2403.06789, Mar 2024): MRR@10 above 40 on MS MARCO dev, +2% out-of-domain BEIR (authors).
candidates.cpu_feasible: SPLADE inference on CPU for queries is fine; document encoding slow.

Leaderboard (self-reported) top: Mira 66.9 (2026-04-22), INF-X-Retriever 63.4 (2025-12-20), RakanEmbed4B 52.4, NVIDIA NeMo agentic 50.9 (2026-03-13), DIVER-v3-GroupRank 46.8, BGE-Reasoner-0928 46.4.

papers.title: Qwen3 Embedding: Advancing Text Embedding and Reranking Through Foundation Models
papers.key_result: 0.6B/4B/8B embedders and rerankers, Apache-2.0; 8B embedder #1 on MTEB multilingual at 70.58 on 2025-06-05 (model-card claim).

papers.title: MMTEB: Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark

papers.title: M3-Embedding (BGE-M3)

papers.key_result: Contextual retrieval keeps more semantic coherence but costs far more compute; late chunking is cheaper but less complete.

papers.title: Anthropic: Introducing Contextual Retrieval (blog, not a paper)
papers.key_result: Failed retrievals down 35% (contextual embeddings), 49% (plus contextual BM25), 67% (plus reranking); $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching; top-20 chunks best.

papers.title: Fusion Functions for Hybrid Retrieval
papers.key_result: Convex combination of normalised lexical and dense scores beats RRF in and out of domain, is sample-efficient (few labels needed), and RRF is parameter-sensitive.

papers.title: HyDE: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels
papers.key_result: LLM-written hypothetical document embedded for retrieval; beats Contriever and works across languages including Japanese and Korean. INF-X-Retriever authors argue direct intent extraction beats HyDE on BRIGHT.

papers.title: Fact, Fetch, and Reason: A Unified Evaluation of RAG (FRAMES)
papers.key_result: 824 multi-hop questions (count from memory, unverified); no retrieval 0.40 accuracy, multi-step retrieval pipeline 0.66.

papers.title: MultiHop-RAG: Benchmarking RAG for Multi-Hop Queries
papers.key_result: News-based multi-hop benchmark; existing RAG retrieves and answers multi-hop queries poorly.

papers.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? (Self-Route)
papers.key_result: Long context beats RAG on average when resourced, but RAG is far cheaper; Self-Route routes per query and keeps long-context quality at lower cost.

papers.title: Long Context vs. RAG for LLMs: An Evaluation and Revisits
papers.key_result: Long context generally beats RAG on Wikipedia-style QA; summarisation-based retrieval matches long context; chunk-based retrieval lags; RAG wins on dialogue and general queries.

papers.title: Language agents achieve superhuman synthesis of scientific knowledge (PaperQA2, LitQA2)
papers.key_result: Agentic RAG with cited answers matches or exceeds experts on literature tasks; about 70% of 2.34 contradictions per paper validated.

papers.title: OpenScholar: Synthesizing Scientific Literature with Retrieval-augmented LMs
papers.key_result: Datastore of 45M open-access papers; GPT-4o hallucinated citations 78-90% of the time while OpenScholar citation precision was comparable to experts; 8B beats GPT-4o by 5% and PaperQA2 by 7% on ScholarQABench (about 3,000 queries).

findings: Reasoning-retrieval state of the art (BRIGHT, self-reported leaderboard fetched 2026-09-30): Mira-Reasoning-Retrieval 66.9 (2026-04-22, weights but no code), INF-X-Retriever 63.4 (2025-12-20, Apache-2.0), RakanEmbed4B 52.4, NeMo agentic 50.9, DIVER-v3 46.8, BGE-Reasoner-0928 46.4 (fully reproducible, MIT). Earlier-era figures for scale: best plain embedder on BRIGHT about 18-30 nDCG@10, ReasonEmbed-8B 38.1, ReasonIR-8B 29.9. Every top entry uses an LLM query rewriter (7B class) plus a 4-8B embedder and often LLM rerankers; none is CPU-feasible at query time without a GPU. Leaderboard entries are not independently verified.

The cheap, CPU-compatible BRIGHT lever is query rewriting: the BRIGHT paper found explicit reasoning about the query gives up to +12.2 points, and BGE-Reasoner runs BM25 over 5 LLM rewrites (top-2000 each, scores summed). Our existing LLM query rewrite plus BM25 is on the right path; add multi-rewrite score summing and test a 'reasoning rewrite' prompt variant against the BRIGHT math/science splits.

Hybrid fusion: Bruch et al. 2022 find convex combination of min-max-normalised lexical and dense scores beats RRF in and out of domain and needs few labels; BGE-Reasoner's final hybrid uses 0.75 dense / 0.25 BM25 after min-max. Our RRF is a robust zero-tuning default, but an evaluation of a tuned convex combination on our held-out set is warranted once dense vectors exist.

Contextual retrieval (Anthropic, Sep 2024): failed retrievals -35% / -49% (with BM25) / -67% (with rerank); vendor claim, 800-token chunks, about $1.02 per million document tokens via API. Doing it locally at 10-50M chunks is not feasible on CPU and cloud LLMs are excluded for the library, so choose: heading-path/title/section-summary prefixes already in our chunks (cheap), or restrict LLM contextualisation to high-value sources when the GPU desktop exists. Late chunking (Jina) is cheaper but a 2025 comparison found it less complete; it requires a long-context embedder pass over whole documents.

Late interaction: PLAID gives tens to few hundreds of ms on CPU at 140M passages (authors), and Rust NextPlaid offers 2-bit/4-bit PQ with memory mapping. My estimate (not measured): 20M chunks of 400 tokens is about 8 billion token vectors; at 2-bit 128-d (about 36 bytes each) that is about 290 GB, above the 100 GB free disk. So use late interaction as a reranker over BM25/dense top-k or over a curated subset, not as the first-stage index, until storage grows. Small 100-150M ColBERTs (GTE-ModernColBERT 54.67 BEIR, ColBERT-Zero 55.43) are the CPU-friendly ones; Reason-ModernColBERT reached 22.62 on BRIGHT at 150M but is non-commercial.

Dense vectors at 10-50M chunks: a 1024-d float32 vector is 4 KB, so 10-50M chunks is 40-200 GB (my arithmetic). With Qwen3-Embedding MRL (dims 32-4096) truncation to 256-512 dims plus int8/binary or PQ in LanceDB this becomes roughly 2-25 GB. CPU bulk embedding of tens of millions of chunks with a 0.6B model is impractical (throughput unverified); the planned GPU desktop is the realistic embedding site. Keep BM25 (tantivy) as the always-on lane.

Learned sparse: SPLADE-v3 is strong but CC-BY-NC-SA. BGE-M3 provides an MIT sparse head and dense and ColBERT heads in one multilingual model. Seismic (Rust, MIT) is the purpose-built index for learned sparse vectors (sub-millisecond on MS MARCO 8.8M, authors). Encoding documents still needs a GPU; a two-lane design of tantivy BM25 plus Seismic or LanceDB is natural in Rust.

Multilingual leaders with permissive licences (model-card claims, not independently verified by me): Qwen3-Embedding-8B MTEB multilingual 70.58 (Apache-2.0, 2025-06), microsoft harrier-oss-v1 0.6B 69.0 and 27B 74.3 (MIT, 2026), Qwen3-Reranker-8B MMTEB-R 72.94 and CMTEB-R 77.45, BGE-M3 (MIT, MIRACL/MLDR), granite-embedding-311m-multilingual-r2 (Apache-2.0, retrieval 65.2). Avoid for shared use: jina-embeddings/colbert/reranker v3-v5 (CC-BY-NC), SPLADE-v3 (CC-BY-NC-SA), ReasonIR and Reason-ModernColBERT (CC-BY-NC), Gemma and LFM custom licences. I could not retrieve per-language MIRACL (ja, zh, es, fr, de) tables or the live MTEB leaderboard (the HF space does not render via fetch), so a language-by-language head-to-head should be run on our own corpus.

CJK BM25: tantivy needs a real tokenizer for Japanese (lindera-tantivy, MIT) and Chinese (tantivy-jieba, MIT); without them BM25 on those languages degrades badly (expected, not measured by me). Per-language analyzer selection at ingest (language detection per chunk) should be part of the chunk schema.

Agentic search (Search-R1, ReSearch, R1-Searcher, DeepResearcher, ASearcher, WebThinker, Tongyi DeepResearch): all need GPU RL training and mostly target web search. The fixed-corpus BrowseComp-Plus result is the useful independent evidence: Search-R1 with BM25 scores 3.86% versus GPT-5 55.9% with BM25 and 70.1% with Qwen3-Embedding-8B. Two lessons: a strong LLM driving a multi-call search loop matters most, and dense retrieval over BM25 adds about 14 points on hard multi-hop. For us: a prompted multi-query search loop using the existing Rust search tool, not RL training.

Long-context versus RAG: long context beats RAG on average when a model can hold the whole corpus (Li 2024, Li 2025), but RAG is much cheaper and the library is 3-5 million pages, so retrieval is mandatory. Self-Route-style routing (try retrieval, fall back to a longer context when the model judges it insufficient) is a cheap idea for guided reading of a single book or paper where the full text fits.

Scientific QA: PaperQA2 (9.3K stars, Apache-2.0, active 2026-09) and OpenScholar (45M-paper datastore, citation precision close to experts while GPT-4o hallucinated 78-90% of citations) are the closest precedents for citation-grounded answers; both validate our exact-quote citation checks and answer-leak guard approach. OpenScholar shows 45M-paper scale is workable with a dense datastore plus reranking (authors' numbers).

Evaluation design to copy: BrowseComp-Plus (fixed corpus, separate evidence vs gold documents, retrieval-only and end-to-end tracks, citation accuracy, prebuilt BM25 index), BRIGHT (CC-BY-4.0, small, CPU-runnable BM25 track), MTEB/MMTEB for model selection (500+ tasks, 250+ languages). BRIGHT and BrowseComp-Plus have small corpora, so they cannot measure scale effects like latency or recall loss at 10-50M chunks; build our own held-out audit set from our library with per-language and per-discipline strata.

Not retrieved or only weakly covered: exact LoTTE and MIRACL per-language numbers, MultiHop-RAG and FRAMES retriever leaderboards (only the paper abstracts were read), LongBench results, and stars/commits for some HF-only models. The NVIDIA NeMo Retriever agentic BRIGHT entry (50.9) could not be confirmed from its repository page, which described a document extraction library (Apache-2.0, 2983 stars, GPU required for local processing).

Star counts and pushed_at dates come from gh api (pushed_at is the last push, not necessarily the last commit to the default branch). FRAMES question count (824) is from memory and unverified. No repositories were cloned and nothing was modified.

candidates.name: pdfium-render (Rust crate over PDFium)
candidates.what_it_is: Idiomatic Rust wrapper over Google PDFium. Gives character-level text with bounding boxes, page index, page rendering to bitmaps (for OCR/VLM), WASM. Crate 0.9.4, updated 2026-09-06; 2.76M downloads.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Already our extraction engine. For born-digital books and papers (most of the 10k-title corpus) the PDF text layer plus char boxes is the only source that gives exact page+offset provenance for exact-quote checks; no OCR model is needed. It is also the renderer to feed scan pages to OCR/VLM. PDFium is not thread-safe (crate's thread_safe feature only adds a mutex), so scale by processes or one pdfium instance per worker, not threads.
candidates.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (crates.io); GitHub API shows NOASSERTION because the file is LICENSE.md
candidates.scale_evidence: Crate downloads (2.76M total, ~1.2M recent) from crates.io: adoption evidence only, not a throughput benchmark. liteparse claims 2-5 ms/page using PDFium text extraction (vendor claim, Apple M2 Max, unverified independently).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes. Text extraction only: est. 100s of pages/s on 8 processes (unverified for our files); 3-5M pages likely hours to ~1 day, bound by disk read of 50-250 GB. Rendering pages to images for OCR costs roughly 20-100 ms/page.

candidates.name: pdf_oxide
candidates.what_it_is: Pure-Rust PDF library: text extraction (char/word level), image extraction, Markdown/HTML conversion, table detection, forms, PDF create/edit. No OCR. v0.3.78 (2026-09-08), 20 language bindings, MCP server.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Candidate pure-Rust fast path or second-opinion extractor alongside PDFium (no C dependency, thread-safe by construction, potentially much faster). Claims 99.5% text parity vs PyMuPDF/pypdfium2. Worth testing on our own PDFs for equations, ligatures, CJK, reading order, and broken-encoding files before trusting.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim: 0.8 ms mean/document, 100% pass on 3,830 PDFs (veraPDF, pdf.js, DARPA SafeDocs suites), single-thread, 5x PyMuPDF. Unverified independently; reading order and large-book behaviour not documented.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes; designed for CPU, parallel via rayon/processes.

candidates.name: pdf-inspector (firecrawl)
candidates.what_it_is: Rust library that classifies a PDF as TextBased / Scanned / ImageBased / Mixed by sampling content streams, then extracts position-aware Markdown (headings, lists, tables) without OCR. Python/Node/WASM bindings.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Exactly the routing step we need: decide per book (and ideally per page) whether the text layer is trustworthy or the page must go to OCR/VLM, so the expensive path only runs on scans and broken-encoding pages. Small Rust code base; easy to port the classifier idea into our ingest.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim: classification 10-50 ms, text PDF extraction under 200 ms, 0.470 s median over a 200-PDF benchmark. Unverified independently; star count is high for its age, treat as marketing-driven.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: LiteParse (run-llama)
candidates.what_it_is: Rust-core document parser (Cargo, npm, pip, WASM) using PDFium for spatial text, bundled Tesseract OCR, optional EasyOCR/PaddleOCR HTTP servers; outputs Markdown/JSON with positions and page screenshots.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: A worked example of the same architecture we run (PDFium plus Tesseract fallback in Rust) with bbox provenance. Its own benchmarks show near-zero math performance, which confirms equations need a VLM or LaTeX-aware path; do not use as the math path.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim: 2-5 ms/page PDFium extraction; 0.389 ParseBench, 0.901 opendataloader-bench (Apple M2 Max, Sep 2026, vendor-run). Math-heavy docs near zero per its own README.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes (Tesseract OCR on CPU).

candidates.name: oxidize-pdf
candidates.what_it_is: Pure-Rust PDF toolkit for AI/RAG: parsing, structure-aware chunking with page refs, bboxes, heading context and token estimates, typed elements (Title, Table, CodeBlock), optional Tesseract. v5.2.0, MIT, 115k downloads.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Closest Rust analogue of our chunker (page-aware, heading-aware chunks). Useful as a reference or fallback; no page rasterisation and no layout ML, so no equations.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim: 99.3% parse success on 9,000+ real PDFs; 6,311 docs/s one-page text-only on i7-3770 (that benchmark is PDF generation/serialisation, not extraction). Extraction speed and accuracy unverified. Note repo renamed: bzsanti/oxidize-pdf now 404, use oxidizePdf.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: lopdf
candidates.what_it_is: Low-level Rust PDF object parser/editor (xref, streams, page tree). Not a layout or text-quality engine.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Useful for robust page counting, metadata, repairing or splitting huge PDFs, and reading embedded page labels (printed page numbers vs physical index) for citations. Not a substitute for PDFium text.
candidates.scale_evidence: Widely used crate (download figures not collected); no extraction-throughput claim.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: mupdf-rs / MuPDF / PyMuPDF / pymupdf4llm
candidates.what_it_is: Rust bindings to MuPDF (messense/mupdf-rs), and PyMuPDF / pymupdf4llm Python layers. MuPDF is fast and high quality, including good text and EPUB/XPS support.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: AGPL-3.0 across mupdf-rs, PyMuPDF (10.8k stars, active 2026-09-30) and pymupdf4llm (2.2k stars); a commercial licence is needed from Artifex for non-AGPL use. Fine for a private personal tool, but it contaminates anything you distribute or serve over a network. Keep PDFium as the default; MuPDF only as an optional comparison oracle.
candidates.scale_evidence: No independent benchmark collected.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.

candidates.name: rbook (EPUB) and epub-rs
candidates.what_it_is: rbook 0.7.10 (updated 2026-07-01): Apache-2.0 EPUB 2/3 reader/builder crate. danigm/epub-rs is the older 'epub' crate and is GPL-3.0 (flag).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: EPUBs have no fixed pages, so citations must use spine item + XHTML offset (and the nav page-list where present for print-page mapping). Use rbook plus an HTML/XML text walker; keep MathML/tables whole and convert MathML to LaTeX. Avoid the GPL 'epub' crate.
candidates.scale_evidence: 51,812 crate downloads (crates.io). Small project, single maintainer.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes; trivially cheap.

candidates.name: olmOCR (toolkit, olmOCR-2-7B-1025, olmOCR-bench)
candidates.what_it_is: AI2's PDF-to-text pipeline around a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B (olmOCR-2-7B-1025, FP8 available), trained with unit-test RL rewards. Pipeline v0.4.0 (2025-10-21). Also authors olmOCR-bench (1,403 PDFs, 7,010 binary tests: arXiv math, old scans math, tables, old scans, headers/footers, multi-column, tiny text).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Best fully open (Apache-2.0 code, weights and data) baseline for scans and math-heavy pages; its benchmark is the most relevant public eval for our mix (math, old scans) and its unit-test method is what our held-out audit sets should copy. Needs the future GPU desktop.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor: under $200 per million pages on a GPU; olmOCR-bench 82.4 +-1.1 (vendor-run, README). Independent reruns in other models' cards consistently place it in the low 80s.
candidates.cpu_feasible: No. README: no CPU-only option; needs recent NVIDIA GPU with >=12 GB VRAM.

candidates.name: MinerU 2.x / 4.0 (MinerU2.5-Pro-2604-1.2B)
candidates.what_it_is: Most-starred document parser. Tiered: Flash (native text, CPU), Basic (ONNX/Torch small models, CPU-capable, OCR+formula+table), Standard/Advanced (small models plus 1.2B VLM, needs >=16 GB RAM and GPU for speed). Outputs Markdown/HTML/LaTeX and Content List V1/V2 with stable page/block locators and bboxes. Reads PDF, EPUB, Office, images. MinerU2.5-Pro (2026-04-06) scores 95.69 on OmniDocBench v1.6.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Best open source for equation, table and page-level provenance output (content_list with page index and bbox), and it already has a CPU path and EPUB support. Licence is custom, not OSI: Apache-2.0 plus conditions (separate licence above 100M MAU or USD 20M monthly revenue; must credit MinerU in online services). Acceptable for a personal tutor.
candidates.license: MinerU Open Source License (Apache-2.0 with additional conditions; GitHub shows NOASSERTION). Model card for MinerU2.5-Pro-1.2B says Apache-2.0.
candidates.scale_evidence: OmniDocBench v1.6 95.69 (model card, vendor-run; OmniDocBench is also run by the same lab, opendatalab). Independent olmOCR-bench (AI2 README): MinerU 2.5.4 scores 75.2. Speed: 2.12 fps on A100 via vLLM (model card). No CPU pages/min published for Basic/Flash tiers: unverified.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Partly. Flash and Basic tiers run on CPU; VLM tiers on CPU only via quantised llama.cpp builds and will be very slow. Plan CPU for Flash/Basic on selected pages only.

candidates.name: PaddleOCR 3.x (PP-OCRv6, PP-StructureV3, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6)
candidates.what_it_is: Most-starred OCR project. 3.7.0 (2026-06-11): PP-OCRv6 (tiny 1.5M / small 7.7M / medium 34.5M params, 50 languages incl. Chinese, Japanese, English, Latin-script, 5.2x CPU speedup via OpenVINO per vendor), PP-StructureV3 (Markdown/JSON with cell coordinates), PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (0.9B, 96.33 OmniDocBench v1.6, 111 languages, 2026-05-28). C++ and ONNX deployment; Rust wrappers exist (oar-ocr, paddle-ocr-rs).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: The strongest CPU-capable OCR for CJK (Chinese, Japanese) plus scans, Apache-2.0 end to end. PP-OCRv6 via ONNX Runtime can run in our Rust service (ort crate or oar-ocr) for scan pages on the 9800X3D now; PaddleOCR-VL is the page-level parser once the GPU desktop exists. PaddleOCR-VL's olmOCR-bench old-scans sub-score is only 38.6 (model card), so scans of old books are a weak spot.
candidates.scale_evidence: OmniDocBench v1.6: 96.34 (OmniDocBench README leaderboard, rank 3; vendor-submitted). olmOCR-bench: PaddleOCR-VL (v1) 80.0 by AI2 (independent). CPU pages/min for PP-OCRv6 or PP-StructureV3 not published: unverified.
candidates.cpu_feasible: PP-OCRv6 detection plus recognition: yes (est. 1-3 s/page/core, unverified). PP-StructureV3: slow on CPU (layout, table, formula models; est. several s/page, unverified). PaddleOCR-VL: GPU, or quantised llama.cpp on CPU at very low speed.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: PaddleOCR-VL at scale; PP-StructureV3 for speed.

candidates.name: Docling (+ docling-parse, granite-docling-258M)
candidates.what_it_is: IBM/LF AI project. DocLayNet layout model plus TableFormer, docling-parse (C++ PDF backend, MIT) and optional VLMs (Granite-Docling 258M, SmolDocling). Reads PDF, EPUB (new), Office, HTML. DoclingDocument keeps page, bbox provenance per element; hybrid chunker; formula and code enrichment.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Cleanest document model and MIT licence; good reference for table structure and provenance schema and for hybrid chunking that keeps tables whole. Slow on CPU, and weaker on math than VLM parsers. Granite-Docling is tiny (258M) but English-primary (Japanese, Arabic, Chinese experimental).
candidates.scale_evidence: Tech report (arXiv 2408.09869, 2024, vendor): 225 pages, OCR off, native backend: M3 Max 1.27 pages/s at 4 threads, 1.34 at 16 threads; Xeon E5-2690 0.60 pages/s at 4 threads, 0.92 at 16 threads; EasyOCR adds 30+ s/page on CPU. Older pipeline version; current speed unverified. Independent: opendataloader-bench (vendor-run) scored Docling 0.882; OmniDocBench leaderboard does not list it.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes but slow: about 1 page/s on 8 cores without OCR, so 4M pages would take ~46 days; use only on selected pages or books.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Granite-Docling VLM mode; large speedups for layout/table models.

candidates.name: Marker (datalab-to)
candidates.what_it_is: PDF/EPUB/Office to Markdown/JSON/HTML/chunks. Now built on Surya VLM served by vLLM (NVIDIA) or llama.cpp; optional --use_llm hybrid mode with Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, Ollama. Inline math to LaTeX in balanced mode.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Well-known, good on born-digital papers (83.5% on born-digital subset) but middling overall. Weights are not open-source: README says modified AI Pubs Open RAIL-M, free for research, personal use and startups under USD 5M revenue/funding (figure from README, unverified; Surya/Chandra pages cite different thresholds). Ok for personal use, risk if the tutor is ever commercial.
candidates.license: Code Apache-2.0; weights modified OpenRAIL-M (revenue-limited commercial use)
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor: 76.0 olmOCR-bench (balanced), AI2 README lists Marker 1.10.1 at 76.1; vendor throughput on a B200: 2.9 pages/s balanced, 7.4 fast, 23.7 fast no-OCR. OmniDocBench (older leaderboard row): 78.44 overall. CPU speed not published.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Older versions ran on CPU (slowly); current VLM-based releases are GPU-oriented, CPU via llama.cpp is very slow (Surya: 0.108 pages/s on Apple Silicon).

candidates.name: Surya 2 / Chandra OCR 2 (datalab-to)
candidates.what_it_is: Surya 2: OCR (91 languages, 87.2% pass rate on its own multilingual test), layout, reading order, tables, inline KaTeX math. Chandra 2 (2026-03): full-page VLM, 85.8 olmOCR-bench, 43-language average 77.8%, 90-language 72.7%.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Top accuracy among locally runnable models for French, German, Spanish-class Latin-script books and for old scans; 85.8 is second only to the paid Datalab API (86.7) on olmOCR-bench. Weights are restricted (modified OpenRAIL-M; Chandra page cites free below USD 2M revenue); code is Apache-2.0.

candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor: Chandra 2 on H100 1.44 pages/s (vLLM, 96 concurrent), ~2 pages/s estimated production. Surya 2 on RTX 5090: 5 pages/s (vLLM, vendor). olmOCR-bench scores are vendor-reported (benchmark itself is AI2's). Surya stars 21,430, last commit 2026-09-11, Apache-2.0.

candidates.what_it_is: 0.9B model (0.4B CogViT encoder plus 0.5B GLM decoder, multi-token prediction) with PP-DocLayoutV3 layout stage and parallel region recognition; 8 languages. Released 2026-03-11 (arXiv 2603.10910).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: MIT licence, small, strong benchmark (94.62 on OmniDocBench v1.5; 95.22 on the v1.6 leaderboard, rank 6) and claimed 1.86 pages/s; light enough for a modest GPU desktop or quantised serving. Weaker on olmOCR-bench (75.2), so it is not clearly better on old scans and math than olmOCR. Only 8 languages supported.
candidates.scale_evidence: Model card: 1.86 pages/s PDFs, 0.67 images/s (vendor). OmniDocBench leaderboard README lists it. olmOCR-bench 75.2 marked with asterisk in model card (vendor-run).

candidates.what_it_is: 1B end-to-end multilingual OCR VLM, Apache-2.0, 11 languages, predicts bboxes for embedded images. arXiv 2601.14251 (2026-01-20, revised 2026-06-30).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Highest published speed at high quality: 83.2 olmOCR-bench (above olmOCR 82.4) at 5.71 pages/s on one H100 (~493k pages/day). Best throughput-per-GPU for bulk OCR of the French/Spanish/German/English scan subset once the GPU desktop exists. Only 11 languages; Japanese and Mandarin coverage should be tested.

candidates.name: dots.ocr (rednote-hilab, now studio-dots-ai)
candidates.what_it_is: 3B (1.7B LLM) single VLM for layout plus OCR, 100+ languages, released 2025-07-30, MIT. Outputs layout JSON with bboxes, categories and text; formulas in LaTeX, tables in HTML.

candidates.name: GROBID
candidates.what_it_is: Java service using CRF (default) or DeLFT deep-learning models to extract TEI XML from scientific papers: header metadata, references, body structure, coordinates of elements.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Best CPU-friendly way to get structured metadata and reference lists from the research-paper part of the corpus (title, authors, DOI, citations) with page+bbox coordinates; it is not designed for books, equations as LaTeX, or scans. Java service adds an operational dependency; call it over HTTP from Rust.
candidates.scale_evidence: Docs say CRF mode is fast on commodity hardware and header processing is sub-second; no pages-per-second figure could be fetched (unverified). Evaluated on PMC, bioRxiv, eLife, PLOS.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes (CRF mode); est. several papers/s on 8 cores (unverified).

candidates.name: OmniDocBench (opendatalab)
candidates.what_it_is: CVPR 2025 benchmark (arXiv 2412.07626): 9 document sources, 19 layout categories, 15 attributes; v1.6 main branch adds Hard subset and new matching; leaderboard of 40+ systems with overall, text edit distance, CDM formula, TEDS table, reading order.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Gives a repeatable evaluation harness (formula CDM, table TEDS, edit distance) for our own held-out audit sets. Leaderboard is crowded and saturating (96.91 top), partly lab-submitted, and is dominated by Chinese/English pages; use olmOCR-bench-style unit tests for arXiv math and old scans and build our own per-language sets.
candidates.scale_evidence: Leaderboard v1.6: TeleOCR 96.91, OvisOCR2 96.47, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 96.34, MinerU2.5-Pro 95.75, GLM-OCR 95.22, MinerU2.5 93.04, Gemini 3 Pro 92.91, dots.ocr 90.77, DeepSeek-OCR-2 90.25, HunyuanOCR 89.95, Qwen3-VL-235B 89.78, MonkeyOCR-pro-3B 88.57, MinerU-Pipeline 86.47, GPT-5.2 86.59, olmOCR 85.74, Mistral OCR 85.66, Nanonets-OCR-s 83.61, Marker 78.44 (README summarised by a fetch tool; row values unverified by direct read). Many entries self-submitted.

candidates.name: xberg (formerly Kreuzberg)
candidates.what_it_is: Rust document-intelligence engine, MIT, v1.0 (rebranded from Kreuzberg; v4 LTS kept as kreuzberg-dev/kreuzberg-lts, 17 stars). 107 formats including PDF and e-books; OCR via Tesseract, PaddleOCR (ONNX Runtime) or candle (pure Rust CPU); Markdown/Djot/HTML/JSON/DocTags; 15 language bindings; REST, MCP.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Closest Rust-native all-in-one, including PaddleOCR-ONNX OCR on CPU, matching the owner's Rust preference. Its benchmarks are vendor-run and it is broad rather than deep on math; worth a read for its OCR-fallback chain and ONNX integration code, but too large to adopt wholesale.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claims 'fastest, most precise' with published benchmarks; not independently verified, methodology not read.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes (Tesseract, PaddleOCR ONNX, candle).

candidates.name: oar-ocr, ocrs, rten, ort (Rust OCR/inference)

candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Practical route to run PP-OCRv5/v6 (Chinese, Japanese, Latin scripts) on CPU inside our Rust service, no Python. ocrs cannot do CJK so it is not suitable for the five-language target.
candidates.scale_evidence: Crate downloads only; no accuracy or speed benchmarks found (unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes (ONNX Runtime CPU; est. 1-3 s/page/core, unverified).

candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor: local mode 60+ pages/s, hybrid 2+ pages/s on Apple M4 (unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes.
