findings: Route, do not parse everything with a model. The feasible architecture is: PDFium text layer (char boxes, page index) for born-digital pages; a per-page classifier (idea from firecrawl/pdf-inspector) to send only scanned, broken-encoding, math-heavy or table-heavy pages to OCR/VLM. The PDF text layer is the only source that gives exact-quote page+offset provenance; VLM output needs offsets anchored to generated text plus a page bbox.

Time to process 3-5M pages. CPU text extraction with PDFium on 8 worker processes: vendor-claimed 2-5 ms/page single-core; our files will be slower; plan hours to roughly one day for 4M pages, bound by reading 50-250 GB. Layout-ML pipelines on CPU (Docling) run about 0.9-1.3 pages/s with OCR off (2024 report, old pipeline), so 4M pages would take roughly 35-50 days: only viable for selected pages. CPU OCR (PP-OCRv6 or Tesseract) at an estimated 1-3 pages/s on 8 cores (unverified; PP-OCRv6 claims 5.2x OpenVINO speedup) means 100k scanned pages is roughly 10-30 hours. GPU VLM at 2-6 pages/s per GPU (LightOnOCR-2 5.71 H100, Surya 2 5 on RTX 5090, MinerU2.5-Pro 2.12 A100, GLM-OCR 1.86, Chandra 1.44 H100, MonkeyOCR 0.5-1.4) means 4M pages takes about 8-25 days of continuous single-GPU time if run on everything, so use the GPU desktop on a filtered 10-20% of pages (~400-800k pages, about 1-4 days).

Benchmarks are saturating and vendor-run. OmniDocBench v1.6 top scores are 95-97 (TeleOCR 96.91, OvisOCR2 96.47, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 96.34, MinerU2.5-Pro 95.75, GLM-OCR 95.22), largely self-submitted and Chinese/English weighted. olmOCR-bench (AI2, 7,010 unit tests) is harder and discriminates better: Infinity-Parser2-Pro 87.6 (35B), Chandra 2 85.8, LightOnOCR-2 83.2, olmOCR 82.4, PaddleOCR-VL 80.0, dots.ocr 79.1, Marker 76.0, DeepSeek-OCR-2 76.3, GLM-OCR 75.2, MinerU 2.5.4 75.2, Mistral OCR API 72.0, Nanonets-OCR2 69.5. OmniDocBench ranks do not predict olmOCR-bench ranks (PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 is 96.3 on the former but only 38.6 on the old-scans subset of the latter; GLM-OCR 95.2 vs 75.2). Build our own held-out audit sets with olmOCR-bench-style unit tests per language and domain.

Licence flags. AGPL: mupdf-rs, PyMuPDF, pymupdf4llm, PDF-Extract-Kit, bookokrat. GPL-3: danigm/epub crate; misraj-ai/qalam. Non-commercial: Nougat weights (CC-BY-NC-4.0); MonkeyOCR v1 weights. Revenue-limited modified OpenRAIL-M weights: Marker, Surya 2, Chandra (thresholds quoted as USD 5M and USD 2M on different pages, unverified). Custom: MinerU (Apache-2.0 plus 100M MAU / USD 20M monthly revenue and attribution), HunyuanOCR (Tencent community licence with geographic limits). Clean Apache-2.0/MIT: PaddleOCR and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6, olmOCR, GLM-OCR (MIT), dots.ocr (MIT), LightOnOCR-2, Infinity-Parser2, DeepSeek-OCR(-2), Docling, pdf_oxide, pdfium-render, lopdf, rbook, xberg, liteparse, pdf-inspector, GROBID.

Rust-native picture. Everything model-based is Python. Rust can own: PDFium text extraction and rendering (pdfium-render), routing (pdf-inspector), EPUB (rbook), chunking with page refs (oxidize-pdf as reference), and ONNX-based OCR (ort plus oar-ocr or PP-OCRv6 models). ocrs is Latin-only so unsuitable for CJK. VLM parsers (olmOCR, MinerU, PaddleOCR-VL, GLM-OCR) should run as a separate local HTTP service (vLLM/SGLang) on the future GPU box, called from Rust with page images rendered by PDFium; results stored with page, bbox and source-hash provenance.

Equations, tables, proofs: only VLM parsers produce usable LaTeX and whole tables. Best formula scores on OmniDocBench v1.6 CDM: PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 97.53, OvisOCR2 97.49, MinerU2.5-Pro 97.45, GLM-OCR 97.18. On olmOCR-bench arXiv-math, LightOnOCR-2 scores 89.6 and GLM-OCR 80.7. Rule-based parsers (liteparse, pdf_oxide, docling-parse, pdf-inspector) do not recover math (liteparse README says near zero). Keep the PDFium text for exact citation and store the VLM LaTeX as a separate field linked by page and bbox.

CJK and multilingual: PaddleOCR (PP-OCRv6, 50 languages including Chinese, Japanese; PaddleOCR-VL 109-111 languages) is the strongest open option for Mandarin and Japanese; dots.ocr claims 100+; Chandra 2 reports 43-language 77.8% average with German 94.8, French 93.7, Portuguese 95.2; Surya 2 91 languages at 87.2% pass rate; GLM-OCR only 8; LightOnOCR-2 11; Granite-Docling English-primary. None of these numbers are independently verified on our corpus; test each language on 200-page samples before committing.

EPUB has no pages: cite spine item plus XHTML character offset (and nav page-list to map to print pages when present). Docling and MinerU both now ingest EPUB; rbook (Apache-2.0) is the Rust crate to use, avoid GPL 'epub'.

Tooling caveats from this run: WebSearch budget was exhausted, so sources are gh (GraphQL for stars, last commit, licence, language), crates.io API, Hugging Face model cards, arXiv abstract pages and raw GitHub READMEs fetched through a summarising model. Numbers that came only from README/model-card summaries are vendor claims; leaderboard rows and CPU speeds are marked unverified where not seen directly. Stars and dates are as of 2026-09-30.

Repos that moved or renamed: kreuzberg-dev/kreuzberg is now xberg-io/xberg (v5 line; kreuzberg-lts holds v4); kermitt2/grobid is grobidOrg/grobid; rednote-hilab/dots.ocr is studio-dots-ai/dots.ocr; bzsanti/oxidize-pdf is bzsanti/oxidizePdf. Not found or not checked: TeleOCR and OvisOCR2 (top of OmniDocBench v1.6 but no repo/model card fetched), Youtu-Parsing (77 stars, licence NOASSERTION), FireRed-OCR (297 stars, Apache-2.0, 2026-03-04), PaddleOCR-VL-1.5.
dimensions.tool_limits: WebSearch refused: session budget of 200 searches already used. Used gh (GraphQL batched repo metadata; a few REST searches, one burst hit the GitHub rate limit and was retried with pacing), WebFetch on raw.githubusercontent.com READMEs, crates.io API, Hugging Face model cards and dataset card, and arxiv.org abs/html pages. WebFetch summarises pages through a small model, so table values (especially the OmniDocBench leaderboard rows, olmOCR-bench scores, throughput numbers) are second-hand and marked vendor or unverified. GROBID benchmark pages returned 404, so its throughput is unverified. Docling CPU numbers come from the 2024 technical report (old pipeline). No CPU pages-per-minute figures were found for MinerU Basic/Flash, PP-StructureV3, PP-OCRv6 or Tesseract; estimates in the output are labelled as such. No files were created in any repository and nothing was cloned or installed."]

candidates.name: tantivy
candidates.what_it_is: Lucene-style Rust full-text library: segments, mmap directory, BM25, positions/phrases, zstd/LZ4 doc store, fast fields, pluggable tokenizers, incremental indexing with merge policy. Latest release 0.26.1 (2026-05-10); CHANGELOG on main already lists 0.27.0 with a breaking set_fast() signature change.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Our current BM25 engine. Nothing found that beats it for a Rust, CPU-only, Windows-friendly 10-50M-chunk lexical index. It is also the engine under Quickwit and ParadeDB. Main work is at the edges: per-language tokenizers, keeping raw text out of the doc store to save disk, merge-policy tuning, and commit batching.
candidates.scale_evidence: README (vendor) claims about 2x faster than Lucene on its own benchmark (tantivy-search.github.io/bench; page would not render so the corpus is unverified). Billion-doc use is via Quickwit (vendor). No independent 10-50M chunk benchmark found (unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes, CPU-only by design. Indexing is multithreaded; search is mmap-based, so the OS page cache does the work on 64 GB RAM.

candidates.name: Quickwit
candidates.what_it_is: Cloud-native, object-storage-backed search engine built on tantivy, aimed at logs and traces. Decoupled compute and storage with stateless indexers and searchers.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Shows how tantivy is run at very large scale, including split/merge design. It is a distributed, Kubernetes-oriented system and overkill for one PC. Read the ideas, do not adopt it.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claims only; the README excerpt I fetched has no petabyte figure. Benchmarks unverified.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes, but the design targets clusters and object stores.

candidates.name: SeekStorm
candidates.what_it_is: Rust lexical and vector search library plus multi-tenant server. Sharded indexing, Roaring posting lists, IVF vectors with 8-bit SQ, 6 tokenizers including Chinese segmentation, stemming for 38 languages, real-time incremental indexing, index in RAM or mmap. Release v3.3.13 (2026-09-12).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: The only credible Rust BM25 rival to tantivy. Worth reading for its sharding design and block/skip logic, and as a fallback or second opinion. It is a single-vendor project and its claims are not independently verified.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor: 7x lower query latency and 17x lower P99 than competitors on search_benchmark_game. 5M-doc Wikipedia hybrid test: 305 us lexical, 2.7-6.4 ms vector at 95-99% recall. Claims 35K docs/s and billion-scale support. Hardware not stated in what I fetched; all unverified.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes, with SIMD on x86-64.

candidates.name: BM25S
candidates.what_it_is: NumPy/SciPy BM25 that precomputes scores into sparse matrices. Supports mmap loading. Paper: arXiv 2407.03618 (2024-07-04).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Useful as a fast evaluation baseline and for small shelves. Not a fit for 10-50M chunks: there is no incremental update, so the index must be rebuilt, and Python memory behaviour is heavy.
candidates.scale_evidence: README: 2M docs use 4.36 GB in RAM vs 0.49 GB with mmap; says 8M+ docs are handleable. Speedups are against rank_bm25 and Elasticsearch on small BEIR sets. Nothing at tens of millions.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes

candidates.name: bm25x (LightOn)
candidates.what_it_is: Streaming-friendly Rust BM25 with lazy scoring, add/delete/update without a rebuild, mmap flat binary format, Unicode stemming, pre-filtered search. Optional GPU path.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: A small, young Rust BM25 with an update-friendly design. Worth a glance only if tantivy's merge behaviour ever becomes a bottleneck.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor: 3.5-6x faster indexing than bm25s on CPU; the 815x batch-search figure is GPU-only on MS MARCO 8.8M. Unverified.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes

candidates.name: Lance (format and Rust core, includes native FTS)
candidates.category: Columnar format + vector and FTS indexes
candidates.what_it_is: Rust columnar lakehouse format with versioned fragments, scalar/FTS/vector indexes, and native BM25 (not tantivy). Release v12.0.0 (2026-09-17). Repo moved from lancedb/lance to lance-format/lance.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: This is what our optional LanceDB vectors actually run on. Read it for the IVF_RQ/IVF_PQ implementations, FTS tokenizers (jieba, lindera, ICU, ngram), the optimize() behaviour and fragment layout. It is also the obvious single-store option for chunk text, metadata and vectors together.
candidates.scale_evidence: LanceDB FAQ (vendor) says it targets 10-50 billion rows and 10-30 TB, recommending Enterprise beyond that. No independent 10-50M chunk benchmark found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes. IVF/PQ/RQ builds and queries run on CPU; GPU index build is optional.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Optional GPU vector-index build; nothing required

candidates.name: LanceDB
candidates.what_it_is: Embedded retrieval library over Lance. Vector indexes: IVF_RQ (RaBitQ, about 1/32), IVF_PQ (1/16-1/64, best at dim <=256), IVF_HNSW_SQ (about 1/4), IVF_HNSW_FLAT. Native BM25 FTS. Multivector support (cosine only). Release v0.39.0 (2026-09-17).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Already in our stack. Caveats from the docs: in OSS, new rows stay unindexed until optimize(); FTS docs advise optimize() after about 100k row changes or 20 operations. Lance FTS has no AND/OR boolean operators. Phrase queries need with_position=True and stop words kept. HNSW variants show latency variance under filters, so IVF_RQ or IVF_PQ is preferred for filtered queries. Concurrent writers can fail.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claims 'billions of vectors'; README gives no benchmark numbers. Unverified.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes

candidates.name: Qdrant
candidates.what_it_is: Rust vector DB with mmap/on-disk vectors and io_uring async I/O. Quantization: scalar int8 (4x), binary (32x), PQ (up to 64x), and TurboQuant (docs say from v1.18.0; 4/2/1.5/1 bit = 8x/16x/24x/32x). Also sparse, multivector, and payload full-text filters. Release v1.19.1 (2026-09-04).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Best-documented quantization, rescore and oversampling controls, and a three-tier memory model (pinned quantized, cold originals). A reference design for a quantize-then-rescore pipeline. As a server, Windows is not a first-class target (unverified), and it has no BM25 ranking engine; its sparse vectors can stand in for that.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor benchmarks at qdrant.tech/benchmarks (not fetched). qdrant/vector-db-benchmark is vendor-run (374 stars). Unverified.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Optional GPU-accelerated HNSW indexing (not confirmed in fetched docs)

candidates.name: Milvus (DiskANN index, Knowhere)
candidates.what_it_is: Go/C++ distributed vector DB with a DiskANN index. Docs: PQ codes in RAM at 12.5% of raw vector size by default (range up to 25%), search cache 10%, NVMe recommended. Knowhere wraps FAISS, HNSW and DiskANN. Release v3.0.2 (2026-09-20).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Shows the RAM budget for DiskANN on SSD: 10M x 1024d f32 is 41 GB raw, so about 5 GB of PQ codes in RAM. The full system is too heavy to run on one Windows PC; I found no Windows server build (unverified).
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor docs claim billions to trillions of vectors. No hardware numbers given in the page fetched.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes, but multi-component and heavy.

candidates.name: Microsoft DiskANN (Rust rewrite)
candidates.what_it_is: Rewritten in Rust as a composable library; the legacy C++ lives on the cpp_main branch and is unmaintained. Claims real-time updates (Fresh-DiskANN, IP-DiskANN) with stable recall and no merges or rebuilds. Release v0.59.0 (2026-09-11).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Best Rust-native candidate for an updatable, disk-resident graph index if IVF_RQ recall proves insufficient. Streaming-update claims match our incremental-ingest need. The Rust disk provider is still being built to match the 2019 NeurIPS numbers. Windows status unknown (unverified).

papers.title: RaBitQ: Quantizing High-Dimensional Vectors with a Theoretical Error Bound for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.key_result: D-dimensional vectors become D-bit strings with a sharp error bound; distance estimation by bitwise/SIMD ops; beats PQ variants in accuracy-efficiency tradeoff (SIGMOD 2024). Gao and Long.

papers.title: Practical and Asymptotically Optimal Quantization of High-Dimensional Vectors in Euclidean Space for ANN Search (Extended RaBitQ)
papers.key_result: Multi-bit extension with flexible space-accuracy tradeoff; claimed asymptotically optimal and better than baselines at equal memory. Library says 4/5/7 bits give about 90/95/99% recall without rerank (authors' claim).

papers.title: TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate
papers.key_result: Random rotation plus per-coordinate scalar quantizers; within about 2.7x of the information-theoretic bound; beats PQ recall with near-zero indexing time. ICLR 2026. Adopted in Qdrant (docs: v1.18.0+) and turbovec. Any dispute about comparisons with RaBitQ is unverified by me.

papers.title: MUVERA: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings
papers.key_result: Turns multi-vector similarity into single-vector MIPS via fixed dimensional encodings; with 2-5x fewer candidates at comparable recall, and on BEIR 10% higher recall with 90% lower latency (authors). Weaviate implementation: 119k-doc set went from 15M vectors (about 8 GB) to 119k FDEs of 2,560 dims, memory about -70%, recall needs ef over 512 to reach 80%+ and near 2,048 for 90%+.

papers.title: PLAID: An Efficient Engine for Late Interaction Retrieval
papers.key_result: Centroid interaction and pruning: up to 7x lower latency on GPU and 45x on CPU vs vanilla ColBERTv2; tens to a few hundred ms on CPU at 140M passages (authors' hardware).

papers.title: ColBERTv2: Effective and Efficient Retrieval via Lightweight Late Interaction
papers.key_result: Residual compression cuts late-interaction space footprint 6-10x. I recall roughly 20-36 bytes per token vector; not verified this session.

papers.title: Reducing the Footprint of Multi-Vector Retrieval with Minimal Performance Impact via Token Pooling
papers.key_result: Clustering-based token pooling gives 50% storage reduction with virtually no loss; 66-75% fewer vectors with under 5% degradation on most datasets.

papers.title: Jina-ColBERT-v2: A General-Purpose Multilingual Late Interaction Retriever
papers.key_result: Multilingual ColBERT with smaller output-dimension options (I recall 128/96/64; not verified here); relevant to multilingual multi-vector storage cost.

papers.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning
papers.key_result: Nested embeddings can be truncated; up to 14x smaller and up to 14x faster large-scale retrieval on ImageNet-1K (authors). Needs an MRL-trained embedding model to truncate safely.

papers.title: LEANN: A Low-Storage Vector Index
papers.key_result: Recomputes embeddings on the fly and prunes the graph; index up to 50x smaller than conventional indexes (about 5% of raw data). Needs an embedding model at query time, so it is a later-stage option for the GPU desktop.

papers.title: BM25S: Orders of magnitude faster lexical search via eager sparse scoring
papers.key_result: Up to 500x faster than popular Python BM25, and faster than some Java-based systems (author's benchmarks on BEIR sets).

papers.title: Better Binary Quantization (BBQ) in Lucene and Elasticsearch (vendor blog, not a paper)
papers.key_result: 32x compression; 138M x 1024d MS MARCO on one 64 GB node: 535 GB to 19 GB, about 12 h indexing, 18 ms and 451 QPS at 70% recall (k=10, 100 candidates, 50 rerank). Vendor numbers.

papers.title: PipeANN: Achieving Low-Latency Graph-Based Vector Search via Aligning Best-First Search Algorithm with SSD (OSDI 2025)
papers.key_result: 1B vectors under 1 ms top-10 at 90% recall, about 40 GB RAM, 20K QPS; insert/delete with 1.07x fluctuation (authors, NVMe Samsung PM9A3).

findings: RECOMMENDATION: keep tantivy as the lexical engine. It is the only Rust BM25 with years of production use, Windows-friendly, mmap-based and with incremental segments. I found no independent benchmark at 10-50M chunks for any engine, so prototype early: ingest 1M then 10M real chunks, record index size, merge time and p95 latency on this PC before committing.

DISK IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT, not CPU or RAM. Estimates (mine, unverified): 10M chunks x 400 tokens is about 4B tokens, roughly 17-18 GB raw text; 50M chunks is about 20B tokens and 85-90 GB raw text. With about 100 GB free, do not keep full chunk text in both the tantivy doc store and a separate store. Store chunk text zstd-compressed once (about 3x smaller, typical) and keep only ids or offsets in the index. A positional tantivy index is commonly a large fraction of raw text size, so 50M chunks will not fit alongside the PDFs on this disk without external storage.

VECTOR MEMORY ARITHMETIC (bytes per vector x vectors). 1024d: f32 4096 B = 41.0 GB at 10M and 204.8 GB at 50M; f16 20.5 / 102.4 GB; int8 10.2 / 51.2 GB; 4-bit RaBitQ or TurboQuant about 512 B plus a small correction term = about 5.2 / 26 GB; 1-bit 128 B = 1.28 / 6.4 GB. 768d: f32 30.7 / 153.6 GB; 1-bit 0.96 / 4.8 GB. Matryoshka-truncated 256d int8 256 B = 2.56 / 12.8 GB. IVF-PQ with 64 bytes per vector = 0.64 / 3.2 GB. HNSW level-0 links at M=16 are about 128 B per vector = 1.3 / 6.4 GB on top of vectors. Milvus DiskANN default keeps PQ codes at 12.5% of raw size in RAM: about 5 GB at 10M x 1024d f32.

RECOMMENDED VECTOR TIER ON THIS PC: 1-bit or 4-bit RaBitQ-family codes (Lance IVF_RQ, about 1/32) held in RAM or mmap, with rerank from an int8 or f16 copy on disk. At 50M x 1024d, 1-bit codes are 6.4 GB; 4-bit about 26 GB; an f16 rerank copy is 102 GB, so rerank from int8 (51 GB) or recompute embeddings for the top 100 instead. For 10M chunks the f16 rerank copy (20 GB) is affordable. Qdrant's docs show the same quantize, oversample and rescore pattern as a reference design.

RaBitQ vs TurboQuant: both are training-free rotation-based quantizers in the same family. RaBitQ has the larger ecosystem (RaBitQ-Library's own README lists Milvus, FAISS, Elasticsearch, Lucene, LanceDB, Qdrant, Weaviate and others; self-reported) and is what Lance's IVF_RQ uses. Qdrant docs list TurboQuant (v1.18.0+). The turbovec README only tested 100K vectors. Do not choose on hype; run our own recall-at-k versus full-precision on held-out queries.

LANCE/LANCEDB OPERATIONAL RULES (from docs): (1) new rows stay unindexed until optimize(); FTS docs suggest optimize() after about 100,000 row changes or 20 operations; unindexed rows are searched by flat scan, so batch ingest then optimize. (2) FTS is Lance-native BM25, not tantivy. (3) Lance FTS has no AND/OR boolean operators, and phrase queries need with_position=True and remove_stop_words=False. (4) IVF_PQ fits dimension <=256; IVF_HNSW variants show latency variance under metadata filters, so use IVF_RQ or IVF_PQ for per-source-rights filtering. (5) Many concurrent writers can fail; funnel writes through one process.

INCREMENTAL-UPDATE BEHAVIOUR: tantivy: append-only segments merged in the background, deletes by term or opstamp; good for BLAKE3-hash incremental ingest. Lance: versioned fragments, optimize() folds new rows into indexes. DiskANN (Rust): claims real-time inserts/deletes with stable recall and no merges. PipeANN and SPFresh: in-place updates on SSD. FastPlaid and NextPlaid: buffered centroid expansion, add/delete without a full rebuild. turbovec: O(1) add and delete by id. BM25S: no incremental update documented, so rebuild only.

MULTI-VECTOR (COLBERT) COST is the main trap. A 400-token chunk yields about 400 token vectors. At 128d with about 36 B each after residual compression (my recollection of ColBERTv2, unverified), 10M chunks need about 4B vectors, roughly 144 GB, and 50M chunks about 720 GB. That cannot fit on 100 GB of free disk. Token pooling (arXiv 2409.14683) cuts storage by 50% with no real loss, or 66-75% fewer vectors with under 5% loss. MUVERA FDEs give one vector per chunk: Weaviate's example uses 2,560 dims (10 KB in f32, so about 100 GB for 10M chunks before compression). Recommendation: do not store multi-vectors for the whole library. Use ColBERT-style scoring only as a rerank over top 50-200 candidates by re-encoding their text, or for a small hot shelf, until the GPU desktop exists.

LATENCY EVIDENCE TO TRUST (all vendor or author-run, none on Ryzen 9800X3D): SeekStorm 5M-doc hybrid Wikipedia: 305 us lexical, 2.7-6.4 ms vector at 95-99% recall; Elastic BBQ 138M x 1024d, 64 GB node: 18 ms, 451 QPS at 70% recall; PLAID CPU at 140M passages: tens to a few hundred ms; NextPlaid CPU P95 219-454 ms; PipeANN 1B vectors under 1 ms on NVMe with about 40 GB RAM. There is no independent benchmark for 10-50M chunks on a desktop-class CPU in what I could reach. Measure ourselves.

PERFORMANCE INTUITION FOR THE 9800X3D (64 GB RAM): at 10M chunks an int8 or 1-bit vector set plus a tantivy index fits in page cache, so queries should be memory-speed. At 50M chunks the BM25 index (tens of GB) will be partly cache-resident, and the 96 MB V-cache helps hot posting lists. This is inference from sizes, not a measurement.

CJK SEGMENTATION OPTIONS for tantivy: Japanese: lindera (MIT; IPADIC, IPADIC NEologd, UniDic, ko-dic, CC-CEDICT, Jieba dictionaries; 10-20 MB/s single-threaded; lindera-tantivy adapter, 70 stars, MIT). Alternatives: vibrato (Apache-2.0, fast, trainable, but last release 2025-03 and no confirmed maintained tantivy adapter), Vaporetto and tantivy-tokenizer-tiny-segmenter (named in the tantivy README; not assessed). Chinese: jieba-rs 0.11.0 via tantivy-jieba or cang-jie (both MIT, recently pushed), using cut_for_search for recall. Lance FTS already exposes Jieba, Lindera (ipadic, ko-dic), ICU and ngram tokenizers. Robust fallback for both: index a second field with character bi-grams (tantivy NgramTokenizer) so segmentation errors cannot cause misses. Use one field per language, routed by language detection at ingest, never one shared analyzer. Bundled dictionaries add tens of MB to the binary; check dictionary licences before redistributing (unverified).

EUROPEAN LANGUAGES: tantivy stems 17 Latin-script languages (README). Lance FTS stems 18 languages including Spanish, French, German, and has stop lists for 13. Per-language fields with stemming plus a stemming-free exact field keep quoted-phrase citation checks exact.

LICENCE FLAGS: AGPL-3.0: ParadeDB, oramacore, kemingy/rabitq; VectorChord is AGPLv3 or ELv2; Typesense GPL-3.0; Elasticsearch GitHub licence NOASSERTION (custom, check); Weaviate, Meilisearch and VectorChord-bm25 show NOASSERTION on GitHub (check before embedding). Clean permissive picks: tantivy (MIT), Lance and LanceDB (Apache-2.0), SeekStorm (Apache-2.0), DiskANN (MIT), lindera and jieba-rs (MIT), RaBitQ-Library (Apache-2.0), NextPlaid (Apache-2.0), Qdrant (Apache-2.0).

WINDOWS NOTE: tantivy, Lance/LanceDB, SeekStorm and USearch are the easy Windows targets. Milvus (distributed, Go), PipeANN (Linux I/O stack) and Qdrant as a server are not first-class on Windows as far as I could confirm (unverified). This favours staying on tantivy and Lance for the next phase.

dimensions.tool_limits: WebSearch was refused (budget of 200 calls already used), so there was no open-web search. Used gh GraphQL (stars, last-commit dates, licences, languages, latest releases for about 90 repos) and gh repo search. Searches were rate limited on the first attempt and succeeded on a paced retry. WebFetch was used for arxiv abstract pages, raw GitHub READMEs and vendor docs. WebFetch summaries come from a small model, so figures are as reported by that summary and some pages lacked the detail I wanted (lindera dictionary licences, tantivy benchmark corpus, SeekStorm hardware, tantivy 0.27 release status, Qdrant and FAISS scale numbers). The tantivy search-benchmark-game page, the Lance FTS format page, SeekStorm ROADMAP.md and a VectorChord blog URL returned 404 or empty content. No independent benchmark at 10-50M chunks was found. Bytes-per-token, compression ratios and disk estimates in findings are my arithmetic or recollection and are marked unverified where they are not from a fetched source. Nothing was cloned, installed or modified."

candidates.name: LightRAG
candidates.category: graph RAG (entity/relation graph + vectors, dual-level retrieval)
candidates.what_it_is: Python GraphRAG that LLM-extracts entities and relations per chunk, stores them in graph plus vector stores, and answers with local (entity), global (relation) and hybrid modes. Latest release v1.5.7 (2026-09-02). Supports Postgres, MongoDB, OpenSearch, Milvus, Qdrant, Neo4j, Memgraph backends, rerankers, document deletion with rebuild from cached LLM responses, and a RAG-Anything merge for tables/equations via MinerU/Docling.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Best-maintained full graph pipeline with true incremental insert (no community rebuild), which matters for growth. Extraction is one LLM call per chunk (default 1200-token chunks, 1 gleaning pass), so whole-library use is very expensive. Worth reading for prompts and storage abstractions; practical only on a small curated subset (e.g. per-course shelves). Its graph would reference chunk ids, so our page/offset provenance is preserved only if we keep our chunk ids as the source ids.
candidates.license: MIT (code); the paper is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper (vendor): win rates vs NaiveRAG 60-84.8% and vs GraphRAG 49.6-52.8% on 4 corpora of 0.6-5M tokens (arXiv 2410.05779, GPT-4o-mini judge). Independent: NodeRAG paper measured 39-90 min indexing for 1.4-1.9M-token corpora; HippoRAG-2 authors measured 68.5M input tokens on MuSiQue (11,656 short passages), about 7.4x HippoRAG 2. Docs say default in-memory storage is test-only. No evidence found of runs at 10M+ chunks (unverified).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Query side and storage yes; indexing needs an LLM. README suggests Qwen3-30B-A3B as minimum local extraction model, which is not practical on CPU at our volume.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Local LLM extraction (vLLM-class serving) and local embedding/rerank on the second desktop.

candidates.name: Microsoft GraphRAG (standard and fast index, global/local/DRIFT/basic search)
candidates.what_it_is: Microsoft's reference GraphRAG: 600-token TextUnits, LLM entity/relationship/claim extraction, Leiden communities, LLM community reports, then Global, Local, DRIFT and Basic search. v3.2.0 (2026-09-24). Has an index method 'fast' that uses NLP noun-phrase extraction plus co-occurrence instead of LLM extraction, but still uses the LLM for community reports. The repo README says it is largely in maintenance mode.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Only approach aimed at corpus-wide 'global' questions (themes across many books). Standard indexing is the most expensive option here; docs say graph extraction is about 75% of indexing cost and warn to 'start small'. The fast method is the only affordable variant and its NLP extraction idea can be reimplemented in Rust. Global search at scale is unaffordable without lazy/dynamic selection (ArchRAG paper measured 1,394M tokens per 100 GraphRAG-Global questions on HotpotQA, about 14M per question).
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor paper (arXiv 2404.16130): ~1M-token podcast corpus took 281 min with GPT-4-turbo; 8,564 nodes. Independent: Commercial Tax paper (arXiv 2608.16096, 2026-08-17) reports published GraphRAG cost of $0.41-$4.42 per MB at gpt-4o-mini batch prices and $3.46/MB by token reconstruction. GraphRAG-Bench textbook study (arXiv 2506.02404) found accuracy 72.50% vs BM25 about 71.7%. HippoRAG-2 authors counted 115.5M input tokens on MuSiQue. No 10M-chunk run found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Fast method's NLP stage runs on CPU; community reports need an LLM. Leiden clustering itself scales but needs a graph store beyond memory at tens of millions of nodes.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: LLM extraction and community-report generation (local model); embeddings.

candidates.name: LazyGraphRAG (Microsoft Research)
candidates.what_it_is: Approach announced 2024-11-25: index with NLP noun-phrase extraction and co-occurrence only (no LLM at index time), then build community structure and do LLM relevance testing and summarization lazily at query time with a budget knob. Editor's note (2025-06-06) says it is being integrated into Microsoft Discovery and Azure Local.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: The design that fits our economics: indexing cost equals vector RAG (vendor claim: 0.1% of full GraphRAG), all LLM spend is deferred to the queries that need it. Vendor claims it outperforms vector RAG, RAPTOR, DRIFT and GraphRAG on local and global queries at 4% of GraphRAG global query cost, and 700x cheaper at comparable quality. The technique can be approximated with our BM25 hits: extract concepts from top-K chunks, build a co-occurrence graph on the fly, and summarize only relevant communities. I could not confirm that the OSS graphrag repo ships it (docs overview did not mention it); treat as unverified.
candidates.license: not applicable (blog and product; no standalone repo found; gh search found only 1-star third-party re-implementations)
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor only: 5,590 AP news articles, 100 synthetic queries (50 local, 50 global), compared with 8 methods. No independent replication or large-scale run found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes for indexing (NLP only). Query time needs a cloud or local LLM.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Nothing at indexing; query-time LLM only.

candidates.name: HippoRAG 2
candidates.category: graph RAG (OpenIE triples + Personalized PageRank, multi-hop)
candidates.what_it_is: ICML 2025 paper 'From RAG to Memory'. LLM OpenIE extracts triples per passage; a graph of phrase and passage nodes with dense-retrieval seeding and Personalized PageRank (PPR) ranks passages. Supports OpenAI-compatible APIs, local vLLM (Llama-3.3-70B tested), Parquet/Qdrant/Chroma/Milvus vector stores, and adding documents without full reprocessing.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Cheapest of the LLM-extraction graph methods with the strongest independent multi-hop evidence (Han et al. found best multi-hop and temporal results). PPR over a graph is easy to port to Rust. Still costs roughly 5-7x corpus tokens in and 1.6-2.4x out per pass, so run only on selected shelves. Note NV-Embed-v2 (its default embedder) is non-commercially licensed per arXiv 2608.16096.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors: MuSiQue 11,656 passages took 9.2M input + 3.0M output tokens and 99.5 min with Llama-3.3-70B; F1 NQ 63.3, PopQA 56.2, MuSiQue 48.6, 2Wiki 71.0, HotpotQA 75.5, NarrativeQA 25.9, vs NV-Embed-v2 61.9/55.7/45.7/61.5/75.3/25.7. Independent (Han et al., arXiv 2502.11371): HotpotQA F1 63.01 vs RAG 60.04; MultiHop-RAG temporal 49.91 vs 30.70; RAG wins single-hop NQ (64.78 vs 63.01 for community GraphRAG) and null queries. Extrapolating 99.5 min per 11,656 passages to 10M chunks gives about 59 days on the authors' setup (my arithmetic, unverified on our hardware).
candidates.cpu_feasible: PPR and graph ops yes; OpenIE needs an LLM (not feasible on CPU at our scale).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: OpenIE LLM extraction and dense embeddings.

candidates.name: RAPTOR (reference implementation)
candidates.what_it_is: Recursively embeds chunks, clusters them (UMAP plus GMM), summarizes clusters with an LLM, and repeats to build a tree; retrieval queries all tree levels. Paper (2024-01-31) reports +20% absolute accuracy on QuALITY with GPT-4.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Closest fit to per-book hierarchical summaries and the cheapest LLM-built structure measured on textbooks: about 10M tokens for a roughly 9-10M-token corpus (about 1x corpus), and best accuracy in GraphRAG-Bench (73.58% vs 70.68% no-retrieval and about 71.7% for BM25). Clustering is per document, so it parallelizes per book and can be built lazily. Repo is stale; reimplement rather than depend on it.
candidates.scale_evidence: Independent: GraphRAG-Bench (arXiv 2506.02404) on 20 textbooks, about 7M words: RAPTOR used about 10M tokens but had the longest build time (20,396 s). HippoRAG-2 authors: RAPTOR 100.5 min on MuSiQue. No evidence at 10k-book scale.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Clustering and embedding yes; summarization needs an LLM.

candidates.name: BookRAG
candidates.category: hierarchical tree plus entity graph for books, agentic query
candidates.what_it_is: arXiv 2512.03413 (2025-12-03). BookIndex combines a table-of-contents-style hierarchy with an entity relation graph, parsed with MinerU layout analysis, and an agent-based query method inspired by Information Foraging Theory.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: The only method designed specifically for books and handbooks with heading hierarchy, which matches our heading-path chunks. It reports much better recall than flat graph baselines but only on tiny sets (85-500 documents) and does not report indexing cost. AGPL-3.0: read for ideas, do not copy code into the service.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors only: MMLongBench (85 docs, 2.8M tokens) EM 43.8 vs DocETL 27.5; M3DocVQA 61.0 vs GraphRanker 43.0; retrieval recall 57.6 vs 26.4 on MMLongBench; query tokens under 5M vs 53M+ for DocETL. No indexing-cost numbers and no large-scale evidence.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Unknown; MinerU parsing and LLM/VLM extraction are GPU-oriented.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: MinerU layout models, VLM for figures, extraction LLM.

candidates.name: ArchRAG (attributed-community hierarchical RAG)
candidates.what_it_is: AAAI 2026 paper (arXiv 2502.09891, v final 2026-05-11): attributed communities plus LLM-based hierarchical clustering, C++ core with Python. Claims better accuracy and lower token cost than GraphRAG.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Gives the clearest query-cost contrast: 5.1M tokens per 100 HotpotQA questions vs 1,394M for GraphRAG-Global (250x less). Indexing cost is still about 100M tokens on MultiHop-RAG (about the same as GraphRAG and above HippoRAG), so it does not solve index cost. Small repo, unclear licence.
candidates.language: C++ (repo language tag; reported as Python-facing)
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors: Multihop-RAG accuracy 68.8% vs RAPTOR 59.1%; HotpotQA 65.4% vs 50.3% best baseline (Llama 3.1-8B backbone). ~100M offline tokens on Multihop-RAG (my fetch summary, approximate).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Clustering yes; LLM extraction and summarization no.

candidates.name: NodeRAG
candidates.what_it_is: Heterogeneous-node graph (entities, relations, semantic units, attributes, high-level elements) with graph algorithms for retrieval (arXiv 2504.11544, 2025-04-15).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Independent-style timing table shows about 2-3x faster indexing and half the storage of GraphRAG/LightRAG on 1.4-1.9M-token corpora, but still LLM-based and the repo has not been updated since March 2025.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors: HotpotQA (1.93M tokens) 21 min vs GraphRAG 66 min vs LightRAG 39 min; accuracy HotpotQA 89.50 vs 89.00 vs 79.00; MuSiQue 46.29 vs 41.71 vs 36.00. No large-scale run.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Graph ops yes; extraction needs LLM.

candidates.name: KAG (OpenSPG)
candidates.what_it_is: Ant Group framework (arXiv 2409.13731, 2024-09-10) with LLM-friendly knowledge representation, bidirectional KG-to-chunk index, logical-form-guided reasoning; claims +19.6% F1 on 2Wiki and +33.5% on HotpotQA over baselines. Built on the Java OpenSPG platform.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Heavy platform dependency (OpenSPG, Java) and schema-driven extraction; poor fit for a Rust plus FastAPI service and for a general book library. Last commit January 2026, last release v0.8.0 (2025-06-28). Indexing cost not found.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claims only; deployed at Ant Group for government and healthcare QA (paper). No independent benchmark or cost data found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Unknown; extraction needs LLM.

candidates.name: PathRAG
candidates.category: graph RAG (relational path pruning), LightRAG derivative
candidates.what_it_is: Builds on the LightRAG-style index but retrieves key relational paths with flow-based pruning and path-based prompting (arXiv 2502.14902, 2025-02-18, revised 2025-11-17).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Only changes query-time retrieval over a LightRAG-type graph, so offers no indexing savings. No licence file found; repo quiet since 2025-12.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors: outperforms LightRAG/GraphRAG on 6 datasets across 5 LLM-judged dimensions. No cost or scale data.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Query side yes; indexing needs LLM (same as LightRAG).

candidates.name: MiniRAG
candidates.category: graph RAG for small language models
candidates.what_it_is: LightRAG-family method designed for small LMs: semantic-aware heterogeneous graph index plus topology-enhanced retrieval; claims results comparable to LLM-based systems with 25% of the storage (arXiv 2501.06713, 2025-01-12).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Relevant to the local-model constraint: shows extraction with small (sub-10B) models can work, but evidence is on a small on-device benchmark, not books. Repo last updated 2025-10.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors only, small benchmark; no large-scale or cost-in-dollars data.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Targeted at small models; CPU inference of small LMs is possible but slow at our volume (my estimate, unverified).

candidates.name: StructRAG
candidates.what_it_is: ICLR-track paper (arXiv 2410.08815, 2024-10-11): at query time a router picks a structure type (table, graph, algorithm, catalogue, chunk) and the LLM restructures retrieved documents before answering.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Zero indexing cost by design; a pattern for query-time graph/table construction over top-K BM25 hits. Code repo is research-grade, no licence. Good idea to copy, not code.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors claim state of the art on knowledge-intensive tasks (Loong, Podcast Transcripts); no independent replication or cost numbers found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes apart from the LLM calls.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Query-time LLM only (router was fine-tuned in the paper).

candidates.name: LinearRAG (Tri-Graph, LLM-free graph construction)
candidates.what_it_is: arXiv 2510.10114 (2025-10-11, v4 2025-11-09): relation-free hierarchical 'Tri-Graph' built from spaCy NER plus embedding linking, with two-stage retrieval (entity activation then passage aggregation by global importance). Zero LLM tokens at indexing, linear in corpus size.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Shows the affordable direction: a graph layer built on CPU that still helps multi-hop. Claims to beat HippoRAG/GraphRAG variants on 2Wiki, HotpotQA, MuSiQue and a Medical set (authors only). GPL-3.0 means clean-room reimplementation in Rust if used. NER is language-specific; we need five more languages (spaCy has es, fr, de, ja, zh models; quality on math-heavy text unverified).
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors only: four datasets; linear-scaling claim not demonstrated at 10M chunks (unverified). Related CPU-only papers: SPRIG (arXiv 2602.23372, 2025-12-27, NER co-occurrence plus PPR) and EHRAG (arXiv 2604.17458, ACL Findings 2026, zero-token hypergraph, repo yfsong00/EHRAG, 12 stars).
candidates.cpu_feasible: Yes (spaCy NER and embeddings); en_core_web_trf on CPU is slow, so budget is my estimate: days for 2B tokens, unverified.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Nothing required; embeddings and transformer NER are faster on GPU.

candidates.name: GraphRAG-Benchmark (textbook evaluation suite)
candidates.what_it_is: Benchmark behind arXiv 2506.02404: college-level domain questions over 20 textbooks (16 disciplines, about 7M words) including math and programming, scored across graph construction, retrieval and generation.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Closest public analogue to our library and to held-out audit sets; also provides per-method construction token counts. Result to remember: on textbooks graph methods gained only about 1-3 points over BM25 (RAPTOR 73.58, HippoRAG 72.64, GraphRAG 72.50, BM25 about 71.7, no-retrieval 70.68), and DALK and G-Retriever hurt.
candidates.scale_evidence: Independent academic benchmark, 9 methods; construction tokens about 10M (tree), 33M (KG), 84M (rich KG) for the about 9-10M-token corpus.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Scoring yes; running the graph systems needs LLMs.

candidates.name: PaperQA2 (agentic RAG over papers)
candidates.what_it_is: FutureHouse's agentic RAG for scientific PDFs: an LLM agent calls search, gather-evidence (LLM re-ranking and contextual summary per retrieved chunk at query time), and answer tools, with citations keyed to chunk ids, metadata and retraction checks. Version 2026.08.12; supports Docling and Nvidia nemotron-parse PDF readers, any LiteLLM model.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Shows that agentic loops over an existing retriever need no offline LLM indexing; all cost is per query (many LLM calls). Docs suggest pre-indexing for 100+ papers and claim under 1k chunks per answer. Its query-time contextual summarization is the same idea as our conditional rerank plus quote checks. Claims are from the 2024 paper (arXiv 2409.13740: matches or exceeds expert performance on LitQA2-style tasks, 2.34 contradictions per paper, 70% validated), so vendor evidence.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor paper on LitQA2; docs state vector store handles thousands of documents; nothing found at 10M chunks. Docs warn 7B local models perform poorly.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Retrieval side yes; agent needs a strong LLM (API or large local model).
candidates.gpu_needed_for: A local capable LLM if not using an API.

candidates.name: Search-R1 (RL-trained search agent)
candidates.what_it_is: RL framework (arXiv 2503.09516, 2025-03-12) that trains an LLM to issue multiple search queries during reasoning; reports +41% with Qwen2.5-7B and +20% with Qwen2.5-3B over RAG baselines on seven QA sets. Follow-ups in Aug-Sep 2026 (BRIDGE 2609.36505, RLVR for small search agents 2609.28765, PrimeSeeker 2609.35816) are unverified beyond abstracts.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Needs GPU training, so only relevant once the second desktop exists; an untrained strong LLM with a tool loop over our search service (the PaperQA2 pattern) is the practical path now. Repo has no commits since 2025-11.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors only, Wikipedia-scale open-domain QA, not books.
candidates.cpu_feasible: No for training; inference of a 3-7B agent on CPU is possible but slow.

candidates.name: EdgeQuake (LightRAG algorithm in Rust)
candidates.what_it_is: Rust implementation of LightRAG (11 crates, v0.28.5 per its README) using PostgreSQL with pgvector and Apache AGE, Louvain communities, PPR graph walks, six query modes, multi-pass gleaning, and a PDF vision pipeline. Supports Ollama, LM Studio, Anthropic, OpenAI and others.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Only Rust graph-RAG option found and a fit for the owner's Rust preference, but it is a single-maintainer project whose own benchmark (n=200 on a medical set, accuracy 0.792 vs LightRAG 0.786) is vendor-only. Worth reading for how to structure graph extraction and AGE/pgvector storage in Rust; do not adopt as the backbone without a scale test.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claims only (about 200 ms vs 1000 ms query latency); no large-corpus run found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Service yes; extraction depends on the LLM provider.
candidates.gpu_needed_for: Local LLM extraction if not using an API.

candidates.name: HiRAG
candidates.what_it_is: Hierarchical knowledge indexing (LightRAG-derived) with multi-layer entity abstraction and a three-level retrieval.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Another LLM-extraction graph with hierarchy; no cost or scale data found. Low priority.
candidates.scale_evidence: Not verified (repo page only).
candidates.cpu_feasible: No for indexing.

candidates.name: LeanRAG
candidates.what_it_is: AAAI-26 (arXiv 2508.10391, 2025-08-14): semantic aggregation into entity clusters with explicit cross-cluster relations and structure-guided hierarchical retrieval; claims 46% less retrieval redundancy.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Improves the retrieval stage and context size; still needs LLM-built graph. No licence file.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors only, four QA benchmarks.
candidates.cpu_feasible: No for indexing.

candidates.name: GFM-RAG (graph foundation model)
candidates.what_it_is: NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv 2502.01113): an 8M-parameter pretrained graph neural network for multi-hop retrieval, trained on 60 KGs (14M+ triples, 700k documents), zero-shot on unseen corpora. Still needs a KG built per corpus.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Small enough to run on CPU at query time, but graph construction (OpenIE) is still required. Appeared in GraphRAG-Bench; no specific advantage shown on textbooks.
candidates.scale_evidence: Authors: SOTA on 10 datasets; no book-scale evidence.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Inference plausible on CPU (8M params); KG build needs LLM.

candidates.name: nano-graphrag and fast-graphrag
candidates.what_it_is: Small hackable Python GraphRAG reimplementations (nano-graphrag about 1,100 lines; fast-graphrag uses PageRank over a typed graph).
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Useful as readable reference code only. Both have had no commits for 8-9 months (nano 2026-01-27, fast-graphrag 2025-11-01). Stars: nano-graphrag 3,990; fast-graphrag 3,955 (circlemind-ai/fast-graphrag).
candidates.scale_evidence: None found.
candidates.cpu_feasible: Indexing needs LLM.

candidates.name: Anthropic Contextual Retrieval (per-chunk context, not a graph)
candidates.what_it_is: Published 2024-09-19: an LLM writes about 100 tokens of situating context per chunk, prepended before BM25 and embedding. Vendor figures: top-20 retrieval failure down 49% (5.7% to 2.9%) with contextual embeddings plus BM25, 67% (to 1.9%) with reranking; one-time cost $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching at 800-token chunks and 8k-token documents.
candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: A far better cost-to-benefit ratio than whole-library graph extraction and it feeds our existing BM25 directly. Books exceed the 8k-document assumption, so context must be generated from chapter-level summaries. At 400-token chunks the output cost roughly doubles per document token. Output token count (100 per chunk x 10-50M chunks = 1-5B tokens) dominates.
candidates.scale_evidence: Vendor claim only; datasets were codebases, fiction, ArXiv, science papers.
candidates.cpu_feasible: The BM25 side yes; context generation needs an LLM.

findings: BOTTOM LINE: whole-library LLM graph extraction is not justified for a 2B-token library. Independent textbook evidence (GraphRAG-Bench, arXiv 2506.02404) shows graph and tree methods gain only about 1-3 accuracy points over BM25 (RAPTOR 73.58, HippoRAG 72.64, GraphRAG 72.50, BM25 about 71.7, no retrieval 70.68), and math and ethics gained least. Han et al. (arXiv 2502.11371) found plain RAG wins single-hop and detail queries and graphs win only multi-hop and temporal ones. Keep the hybrid BM25 plus vector plus rerank pipeline as the core and add structure selectively.

COST ASSUMPTIONS (mine): corpus is about 2B text tokens (4M pages x about 500 tokens; about 9 GB of text; 10-50M chunks at 400 tokens implies 4-20B tokens only if overlap or smaller pages, so 2B is the low-middle case). Prices from platform.claude.com pricing page fetched today: Sonnet 5.5 $2 in / $10 out per MTok (batch $1/$5); Haiku 4.5 $1/$5 (batch $0.50/$2.50). Claude 4.7+ tokenizers produce about 30% more tokens for the same text, so Sonnet 5.5 figures could be up to 30% higher (unverified for these prompts). All dollar figures below are order-of-magnitude extrapolations, not measurements at this scale.

INDEXING COST 1, full GraphRAG (standard): measured $0.41-$4.42 per MB of text and $3.46/MB by token reconstruction at gpt-4o-mini batch prices (arXiv 2608.16096). 9,300 MB x $3.46 = about $32k at gpt-4o-mini prices; Claude batch prices are about 7x (Haiku 4.5) to 13-16x (Sonnet 5.5) higher, giving about $30k-$300k on Haiku-class batch and up to about $500k on Sonnet-class. HippoRAG-2 authors counted 115.5M input tokens for 11,656 short passages, about 60-90x corpus tokens. Unaffordable, and global search adds about 14M tokens per question (ArchRAG paper).

INDEXING COST 2, LightRAG-style entity/relation extraction: no dollar measurement, but LightRAG used 68.5M input tokens on MuSiQue (about 54x corpus tokens; inflated by short 100-token passages where prompt overhead dominates). On textbook-like chunks GraphRAG-Bench measured 33M tokens (KG) and 84M tokens (rich KG) for a about 9-10M-token corpus, i.e. 3.5x to 9x corpus tokens total. For 2B tokens that is 7B-18B tokens; at in:out 3:1 that is about $7k-$18k on Haiku 4.5 batch and $14k-$36k on Sonnet 5.5 batch, double at standard prices. Plus about 4x-6x more for any further community-report pass.

INDEXING COST 3, HippoRAG-2 style OpenIE: 9.2M input and 3.0M output tokens for 11,656 passages (about 1.27M corpus tokens per arXiv 2608.16096, so about 7x in and 2.4x out per corpus token). For 2B tokens: about 14.5B in and 4.7B out, about $19k (Haiku 4.5 batch) to about $38k (Sonnet 5.5 batch), about $38k-$76k at standard prices. Measured time 99.5 min per 11,656 passages on Llama-3.3-70B; scaling to 10M chunks is about 59 days on the authors' (unspecified) setup, my extrapolation.

INDEXING COST 4, RAPTOR-style summary tree: about 1x corpus tokens measured (10M tokens for the textbook corpus), so about 2B tokens (roughly 1.6B in and 0.4B out): about $2k (Haiku batch) to $3.6k (Sonnet 5.5 batch). Cheapest LLM-built structure measured, best textbook accuracy, but slowest wall-clock in the benchmark (20,396 s), so parallelize per book.

INDEXING COST 5, per-book and per-chapter summaries only (map-reduce over the existing heading tree): roughly one pass of input (about 2.2B tokens with overlap) plus about 55M output tokens (100k chapters x about 400 plus 10k books x about 1.5k): about $1.3k Haiku 4.5 batch or about $2.5k Sonnet 5.5 batch (my estimate). Built lazily only for books that get queried, it is a small fraction of that. Local LLM alternative: about 2B prefill tokens at an assumed 20k tok/s on the planned GPU desktop is about a day (unverified).

INDEXING COST 6, zero-LLM graphs (LazyGraphRAG index, LinearRAG, SPRIG, EHRAG, GraphRAG fast extraction): cost is CPU and embeddings only. Vendor claim: LazyGraphRAG indexing equals vector RAG and is 0.1% of GraphRAG. Wall-clock for spaCy NER on 2B tokens on 16 threads is my estimate of tens of hours with small models and days with transformer NER, unverified; multilingual NER quality (es, fr, de, ja, zh) and on equations/chemistry text is unverified and likely weak. A Rust implementation of a co-occurrence or noun-phrase concept graph from tantivy term statistics avoids NER models entirely but needs validation.

LOCAL-ONLY CONSTRAINT: CPU-only LLM extraction on the 9800X3D is not feasible at this scale (my estimate: a 7-8B model at Q4 generates on the order of 10-20 tok/s, so a few billion output tokens would take years). Whole-library OpenIE or entity extraction would need the second GPU desktop and roughly 1-2 weeks for the light variants (my estimate, unverified). Also note the stated rule bans cloud OCR and embeddings; sending book text to a cloud LLM for extraction or summaries is arguably the same kind of leak and conflicts with per-source rights, so the API dollar figures are a cost comparison only.

RECOMMENDED PRACTICAL ARCHITECTURE: (1) Keep BM25 (plus vectors when available) as the base; fix retrieval with contextual chunk headers from the heading path (free, already stored) before any graph. (2) Build hierarchical structure from the book's own heading tree (TOC) plus lazily generated LLM summaries per chapter and book when first queried, cached by content hash; reserve RAPTOR-style clustering for chapters without usable headings. (3) Add a cheap LLM-free concept co-occurrence graph (LinearRAG, LazyGraphRAG-style) for multi-hop, stored per book and per shelf, in Rust; do not build a corpus-wide entity graph. (4) For global or thematic questions, use query-time graph construction: take the top-K retrieved chunks, extract concepts, cluster, and summarize only relevant communities (LazyGraphRAG and StructRAG pattern). (5) Run full LLM entity graphs (LightRAG or HippoRAG 2) only on small curated shelves (for example 100-500 books in one course) where multi-hop evidence exists. (6) Route by query type (EA-GraphRAG arXiv 2602.03578, Han et al.'s selection strategy): single-fact queries stay on BM25 plus rerank; only multi-hop or global queries trigger graph or agentic paths.

AGENTIC LOOPS: the practical pattern is PaperQA2-style (an LLM agent with search, gather-evidence and answer tools over the existing retrieval service; zero index cost, per-query cost of roughly 10-20 LLM calls, about $0.1-$0.3 per question with a Sonnet-class model by my estimate). It fits our existing citation checks because evidence carries chunk ids. RL-trained search agents (Search-R1 and the Aug-Sep 2026 follow-ups) need GPU training and were evaluated on Wikipedia QA, not books; the open deep-research repos found (langchain-ai/open_deep_research 12.7k stars, archived; bytedance/deer-flow 83k stars; assafelovic/gpt-researcher 29.8k; Alibaba-NLP/DeepResearch 20k) are web-research agents, not library retrievers, so low value for us.

INCREMENTAL INGEST: LightRAG documents seamless incremental insert and deletion with cached LLM responses; HippoRAG allows adding documents without full reprocessing; GraphRAG's community hierarchy needs rebuilding (LightRAG paper claim, vendor), and ArchRAG/RAPTOR-style global trees also need re-clustering. Per-book structures (book tree, per-book concept graph) keyed by BLAKE3 hash are the only design that stays incremental at 10x-100x growth.

LICENCE FLAGS: BookRAG AGPL-3.0; LinearRAG GPL-3.0 (clean-room reimplement if used); Khoj (37.5k stars) is AGPL-3.0 and irrelevant here; NV-Embed-v2 (default embedder in HippoRAG 2 benchmarks) is non-commercial, per arXiv 2608.16096, which also says NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Embed-8B (July 2026) matched its recall (unverified by me); LightRAG paper is CC BY-NC-SA but the code is MIT; PathRAG, LeanRAG, StructRAG, ArchRAG and EHRAG repos declare no licence. Graph DB note: kuzudb/kuzu (embedded graph DB) is archived (last push 2025-10-10).

MATURITY RANKING for our use: production-ish and maintained (LightRAG, Microsoft GraphRAG in maintenance mode, PaperQA2, RAGFlow 91.6k stars Apache-2.0 bundles GraphRAG and RAPTOR but is a full platform and not evaluated here); research-active (HippoRAG 2, LinearRAG, GFM-RAG, BookRAG); stale (RAPTOR since 2024-09, NodeRAG since 2025-03, nano-graphrag, fast-graphrag, KAG since 2026-01). Only one Rust option found (EdgeQuake) and it is single-maintainer with vendor-only benchmarks. Rust is most clearly beneficial for the CPU-side pieces: concept/co-occurrence graph building, Personalized PageRank, per-book clustering, and tree caching, because those touch tens of millions of chunks; LLM orchestration can stay in Python.

EVALUATION: GraphRAG-Bench (MIT, textbook questions, per-stage scoring) is the nearest public proxy for held-out audit sets. Judge bias caveat from Han et al.: LLM-as-judge results flipped when answer order was reversed, so use position-randomized or exact-quote and retrieval-recall metrics, which fit our citation checks.

candidates.what_it_is: Apache-2.0 sparse MoE embedder: 475M total, 305M active (8 experts top-2), 768-d with Matryoshka to 256, but only 512-token context, about 100 languages; open training code (contrastors). Supported in fastembed-rs (nomic-v2-moe candle feature) and TEI.

candidates.why_it_matters_for_us: Retrieval-tuned with explicit MRL and quantization-robustness focus (good for 50M-vector storage). l-v2.0 BEIR 55.65 / MIRACL 66.0, so strong English scientific retrieval with multilingual parity. Older (Dec 2024) and overtaken on MMTEB by Qwen3.
candidates.scale_evidence: Paper arXiv 2412.04506 (2024-12-03). Model-index on l-v2.0: SciFact 70.59, NFCorpus 35.34, ArguAna 59.15. Nomic card: BEIR 55.65, MIRACL 66.0. Vendor/authors' numbers; HF downloads 958k (l), 127k (m).

candidates.what_it_is: English-only Qwen2-1.5B based embedder (MIT), 1.54B params, MRL dims 512-8192; Jasper is a 2B English+vision distillation of stella.

candidates.scale_evidence: No scores verified in this pass (MTEB-Eng only, unverified).

candidates.name: ColPali / ColQwen2 / ColQwen2.5 / ColQwen3 (visual late interaction) and vidore benchmark

Use only as a reranker over top-k page images or for a small scan-heavy subset. Needs GPU (3B VLM).

candidates.what_it_is: Rust inference crate for Model2Vec/potion static models (v0.3.0, 2026-09-19).

findings: Bottom line: CPU-only dense embedding of 10-50M 400-token chunks with any transformer embedder is not practical; it is a GPU-machine job. BM25 stays the primary index now. On CPU, dense is feasible only for (a) the static Model2Vec tier, (b) a small transformer (mE5-small / EmbeddingGemma-300M / Arctic-m-v2 / gte-multilingual-base) on a subset, and (c) query-time embedding and small-k reranking.

Measured CPU data found is thin: MiniLM-L6 1,739 sentences/s and static-retrieval-mrl 107,420 sentences/s on an i7-13700K (HF static-embeddings blog, sentence length not stated); model2vec-rs 8,000/s single-thread; Intel-only int8 speedups up to 4x. No independent measurement of any transformer embedder on a Ryzen 9800X3D or Zen 5 was found. All throughput below is arithmetic and must be replaced by a 5-minute measurement on this PC (e.g. 2,000 real chunks per candidate via fastembed-rs/ort).

Arithmetic method: FLOPs per token = 2 x non-embedding parameters, plus about 5% attention at 400 tokens. Per 400-token chunk: mE5-small (21M non-emb) about 20 GFLOP; EmbeddingGemma-300M (about 107M non-emb) about 90; Arctic-m-v2 / gte-multilingual-base (about 113M) about 95; BGE-M3 (about 303M) about 260; Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (440M) about 372; 4B (about 3.6B) about 2.9 TFLOP; 8B (about 6.95B) about 5.6 TFLOP. Parameter counts from HF safetensors metadata and MTEB page (0.6B: 596M total, 440M active).

CPU assumption (derived, unverified): Zen 5 has 512-bit FP datapaths, so peak fp32 is about 8 cores x 64 FLOP/cycle x about 4.5 GHz = about 2.3 TFLOPS. Assume 1.0 TFLOPS effective for ORT/MKL-class kernels (about 45% of peak) and 0.4 TFLOPS for candle's pure-Rust gemm path. int8 VNNI might add 2-3x (Intel reports up to 4x on Xeon; unverified on Zen 5).

Time to embed at 1.0 TFLOPS effective (chunks/s, then 10M chunks, then 50M chunks): mE5-small 50/s, 2.3 d, 11.6 d; EmbeddingGemma-300M 11/s, 10.5 d, 52 d; Arctic-m-v2 or gte-mult-base 10.5/s, 11 d, 55 d; BGE-M3 3.85/s, 30 d, 150 d; Qwen3-0.6B 2.7/s, 43 d, 215 d; Qwen3-4B 0.34/s, 340 d, 1,700 d; Qwen3-8B 0.18/s, 650 d, 3,200 d. At candle-class 0.4 TFLOPS multiply each by 2.5. Checks: 10M / 2.7 = 3.7M s = 43 d; 10M / 0.34 = 29M s = 340 d.

Same arithmetic on the planned GPU desktop, assuming 60 TFLOPS effective bf16 (an assumption; hardware unknown): Qwen3-0.6B about 160 chunks/s, 10M in about 17 h, 50M in about 3.6 d; 4B about 21/s, 5.6 d and 28 d; 8B about 11/s, 10.8 d and 54 d (ignores padding and attention overhead). GPU pays off only for 0.6B-4B at this scale.

Rust runtime options: ort (ONNX Runtime; best CPU for BERT/XLM-R encoders, int8, but crate is still 2.0.0-rc.13), fastembed-rs 7.1.0 (wraps ort + candle; ships BGE-M3, mE5, EmbeddingGemma, bge-reranker-v2-m3, Qwen3 and Nomic-v2-MoE; ort is a mandatory dependency even for candle-only builds, so you must use ort-download-binaries or ort-load-dynamic), candle 0.11 (pure Rust, needed for decoder models without C++; slower on CPU; MKL optional), TEI 1.9.4 (Rust server, ONNX recommended on x86), llama.cpp/llama-cpp-2 (C++ GGUF, good for Qwen3 Q8/Q4), EmbedAnything 0.7.1 (wrapper, no published benchmarks). Recommendation for the Rust service: fastembed-rs or direct ort for CPU encoders now; candle or TEI container for Qwen3 on the GPU desktop.

Storage, not just compute, constrains the plan with about 100 GB free. 50M vectors x 1024 dims: fp32 204.8 GB, int8 51.2 GB, binary 6.4 GB; with MRL to 256 dims and int8 12.8 GB; 10M x 1024 fp32 is 41 GB. Qwen3-8B at 4096 dims fp32 would be 819 GB for 50M. MRL models (Qwen3, jina v5, nomic v2, Arctic 2.0, EmbeddingGemma, harrier/Nemotron via slicing) and natively int8/binary outputs (pplx-embed) are therefore a selection criterion, and quantization loss must be measured on the audit set. LanceDB supports quantized IVF-PQ indexes (not benchmarked here).

Quality picture (vendor tables, June 2025 to Aug 2026; not independently verified): MMTEB mean task: Qwen3-8B 70.58, Qwen3-4B 69.45, Qwen3-0.6B 64.33, mE5-large-instruct 63.22, EmbeddingGemma-300M 61.15, BGE-M3 59.56; jina-v5-text-small 67.7 and nano 65.5 (NC licence); Harrier 0.6B 69.0 (benchmark variant unclear); Nemotron-3-Embed-1B MMTEB retrieval 71.04. Retrieval-only MMTEB: Qwen3-8B 70.88, 0.6B 64.64, BGE-M3 62.79, mE5-large-instruct 62.61 (Qwen card; two sources conflict on the 4B retrieval figure). Top-of-leaderboard rankings could not be read because the MTEB leaderboard page did not render in WebFetch.

Licences to flag: non-commercial - all Jina weights (v3, v5, reranker v2/m0/v3/v3.5, jina-colbert-v2: CC-BY-NC-4.0; v4: Qwen Research License), ColQwen2.5 (Qwen Research backbone). Custom terms - EmbeddingGemma and bge-multilingual-gemma2 (Gemma Terms; gated), LiquidAI LFM2.5 (LFM Open License v1.0), NVIDIA Nemotron (OpenMDW-1.1; llama-nemotron-embed-1b-v2 'other'). Clean permissive - Qwen3-Embedding/Reranker, BGE-M3 (MIT), bge-reranker-v2-m3, Nomic v2 MoE, Arctic 2.0, gte-multilingual, mxbai-rerank-v2, Granite (Apache-2.0), mE5/potion/Harrier/pplx-embed (MIT). zerank-2 and zembed-1 list Apache-2.0 on HF metadata, but zerank-2 is tagged English-only.

Language coverage for ja/zh/es/fr/de: Qwen3 (100+), BGE-M3 (100+, MIRACL includes all five), Harrier (94), jina v5 (119+), Nemotron-3-Embed (34 evaluated incl. all five), Granite (200+ with 52 enhanced), EmbeddingGemma (100+), gte-multilingual (70+), Arctic 2.0 (74), Nomic v2 (about 100), potion-multilingual (101, weak). LFM2.5 covers es/de/fr/ja but not zh. Stella/Jasper and mxbai-embed are English-only. Per-language nDCG@10 for our five languages was not available except gte-multilingual-base MultiLongDocRetrieval (es 81.2, fr 76.2, de 55.2, ja 52.1, zh 27.4); these differ by dataset difficulty and are not comparable across languages.

Reranking on CPU costs: bge-reranker-v2-m3 about 0.65 GFLOP/token, so top-10 x 256 tokens is about 1.7 s and top-20 x 400 about 5 s; Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B top-20 x 400 about 7 s; gte-multilingual-reranker-base (306M) about 1.6 s (all derived at 1 TFLOPS effective). Keep the existing conditional rerank at k<=10-20 on CPU; larger k or 4B/8B rerankers need the GPU box. Query-time embedding (30 tokens through a 0.6B model, about 28 GFLOP) is cheap at tens of milliseconds, derived.

Static embeddings (potion, sentence-transformers StaticEmbedding) are 60-400x faster than transformers on CPU (HF blog: 397x vs all-mpnet) but lose a lot: potion-multilingual-128M MMTEB 47.31 vs 59-70; English retrieval 35.06 vs MiniLM 42.92. They cannot capture equations or word order, so use them only as an extra first-stage list fused by RRF with BM25, and accept them only if they lift recall on the held-out audit set.

Visual/late-interaction models (ColPali, ColQwen, jina-v4 multi-vector, Qwen3-VL-Embedding) need a 2-8B VLM on GPU and about 1,000 vectors per page. 5M pages x about 1,030 x 128 B int8 is about 660 GB (derived), so use them only as a page-image reranker or for scanned/figure-heavy subsets, not as the main index.

Suggested path: now - BM25 plus optional potion-multilingual static list, int8 mE5-small or EmbeddingGemma-300M on a prioritized subset (headings, definitions, abstracts), bge-reranker-v2-m3 or gte-multilingual-reranker at k<=10. On the GPU desktop - Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (or 4B) with MRL truncation plus int8 storage, Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B/4B, served by TEI or candle; evaluate Harrier-0.6B, Nemotron-3-Embed-1B and Granite-311M-r2 as challengers using the MTEB harness on our own held-out audit set rather than vendor tables.
